author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, A selection from the discourses of epictetus. of the things which are in our power and not in our power
text: Of all the faculties (except that which I shall soon mention), you will find not one which is capable of contemplating itself, and, consequently, not capable either of approving or disapproving.
plain: None of your abilities can look at itself, so none can approve or reject. The one I will name soon can.

author: Epictetus
text: When a man was consulting him how he should persuade his brother to cease being angry with him, Epictetus replied: Philosophy does not propose to secure for a man any external thing.
plain: Someone asked how to get his brother to stop being angry. He heard that this teaching will not get him anything outside himself.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, That we ought not to be angry with the errors (faults) of others
text: Ought not then this robber and this adulterer to be destroyed? By no means say so, but speak rather in this way: This man who has been mistaken and deceived about the most important things, and blinded, not in the faculty of vision which distinguishes white and black, but in the faculty which distinguishes good and bad, should we not destroy him?
plain: Do not say the thief and the cheater should be wiped out. He is blind about good and bad, not about telling colors apart.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How we should behave to tyrants
text: If a man possesses any superiority, or thinks that he does when he does not, such a man, if he is uninstructed, will of necessity be puffed up through it.
plain: If you have an edge, or only think you do, and no one taught you, you swell with pride.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, Against those who wish to be admired
text: When a man holds his proper station in life, he does not gape after things beyond it.
plain: When you keep your proper place in life, you do not long for things beyond it.

author: Epictetus
text: Præcognitions are common to all men, and præcognition is not contradictory to præcognition.
plain: The basic ideas people start with are shared by all. One of those starting ideas does not clash with another.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How we should struggle with circumstances
text: It is circumstances (difficulties) which show what men are. Therefore when a difficulty falls upon you, remember that God, like a trainer of wrestlers, has matched you with a rough young man.
plain: Hard times show the kind of person you are. When trouble hits, God, like a wrestling coach, has paired you with someone rough.

author: Epictetus
text: If these things are true, and if we are not silly, and are not acting hypocritically when we say that the good of man is in the will, and the evil too, and that everything else does not concern us, why are we still disturbed, why are we still afraid?
plain: You say good and bad live in your choices, and the rest is not yours. So why stay upset and afraid.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, In how many ways appearances exist, and what aids we should provide against them
text: Appearances are to us in four ways. For either things appear as they are; or they are not, and do not even appear to be; or they are, and do not appear to be; or they are not, and yet appear to be.
plain: You meet things four ways. They look real and are, look gone and are gone, are real but hidden, or look real but are gone.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, That we ought not to be angry with men; and what are the small and the great things among men
text: What is the cause of assenting to anything? The fact that it appears to be true.
plain: You agree with something because it looks true to you.

author: Epictetus
text: The being (nature) of the good is a certain will; the being of the bad is a certain kind of will.
plain: Good is one way of choosing. Bad is another way of choosing.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, That confidence (courage) is not inconsistent with caution
text: The opinion of the philosophers perhaps seem to some to be a paradox; but still let us examine as well as we can, if it is true that it is possible to do everything both with caution and with confidence.
plain: Some people find it strange, but let us check whether you can do all things with both care and trust.

author: Epictetus
text: Consider, you who are going into court, what you wish to maintain and what you wish to succeed in.
plain: If you are heading into a hearing, decide what you want to hold onto and what you want to win.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How magnanimity is consistent with care
text: Things themselves (materials) are indifferent; but the use of them is not indifferent.
plain: The stuff itself does not really matter. The way you use that stuff does matter.

author: Epictetus
text: The hypothetical proposition is indifferent: the judgment about it is not indifferent, but it is either knowledge or opinion or error.
plain: An if-then claim does not matter by itself. Your judgment of it does, and it counts as knowledge, a view, or a mistake.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How we ought to use divination
text: Through an unreasonable regard to divination many of us omit many duties. For what more can the diviner see than death or danger or disease, or generally things of that kind?
plain: Too much trust in sign reading makes many of us skip our tasks. A sign reader sees only death, danger, or sickness.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, That when we cannot fulfil that which the character of a man promises, we assume the character of a philosopher
text: It is no common (easy) thing to do this only, to fulfil the promise of a man’s nature.
plain: It is not a simple job just to live out what a person is built to be.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How we may discover the duties of life from names
text: Consider who you are. In the first place, you are a man; and this is one who has nothing superior to the faculty of the will, but all other things subjected to it; and the faculty itself he possesses unenslaved and free from subjection.
plain: Think about who you are. You are a person, and nothing sits above your free choice, while all else sits under it.

author: Epictetus
text: What things a man must learn in order to be able to apply the art of disputation, has been accurately shown by our philosophers (the Stoics); but with respect to the proper use of the things, we are entirely without practice.
plain: People have been shown what to learn so they can argue well. We still get no practice at using those things the right way.

author: Epictetus
text: When I see a man anxious, I say, What does this man want? If he did not want something which is not in his power, how could he be anxious?
plain: When I see you worried, I ask what you want. You feel uneasy because that want sits outside your control.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How a man should proceed from the principle of god being the father of all men to the rest
text: If a man should be able to assent to this doctrine as he ought, that we are all sprung from God in an especial manner, and that God is the father both of men and of gods, I suppose that he would never have any ignoble or mean thoughts about himself.
plain: If you really believe you come specially from God, father of people and gods, you never think small of yourself.

author: Epictetus
text: When a certain Roman entered with his son and listened to one reading, Epictetus said, This is the method of instruction; and he stopped.
plain: A man walked in with his son while someone was reading. The teacher said this is how we teach, and then he stopped.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To or against those who obstinately persist in what they have determined
text: When some persons have heard these words, that a man ought to be constant (firm), and that the will is naturally free and not subject to compulsion, but that all other things are subject to hindrance, to slavery, and are in the power of others, they suppose that they ought without deviation to abide by everything which they have determined.
plain: People hear that your choice is free and firm, while other things can be blocked by others. They think they must stick to every plan.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, That we do not strive to use our opinions about good and evil
text: Where is the good? In the will. Where is the evil? In the will. Where is neither of them?
plain: Good and bad both sit in your choice. Ask where neither of them sits.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How we must adapt preconceptions to particular cases
text: What is the first business of him who philosophizes? To throw away self-conceit.
plain: The first job on this path is to throw out thinking too highly of yourself.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How we should struggle against appearances
text: Every habit and faculty is maintained and increased by the corresponding actions: the habit of walking by walking, the habit of running by running.
plain: Every habit grows through the actions that match it. Walking grows by walking, and running grows by running.

author: Epictetus
text: Some things men readily confess, and other things they do not. No one then will confess that he is a fool or without understanding; but quite the contrary you will hear all men saying, I wish that I had fortune equal to my understanding.
plain: People admit some things easily and hide other things. Nobody calls himself a fool, yet all wish their luck matched their smarts.

author: Epictetus
text: What a man applies himself to earnestly, that he naturally loves. Do men then apply themselves earnestly to the things which are bad?
plain: You grow to love whatever you work at with real effort. Do people put that same effort into bad things.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, On the power of speaking
text: Every man will read a book with more pleasure or even with more ease, if it is written in fairer characters.
plain: A book feels nicer, and even easier, when the letters on the page look cleaner.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To (or against) a person who was one of those who were not valued (esteemed) by him
text: A certain person said to him (Epictetus): Frequently I desired to hear you and came to you, and you never gave me any answer; and now, if it is possible, I entreat you to say something to me.
plain: Someone said he often came hoping to hear an answer, and never got one. He asked to be told something now, if possible.

author: Epictetus
text: When one of those who were present said, Persuade me that logic is necessary, he replied, Do you wish me to prove this to you?
plain: Someone there said, convince me that clear reasoning is needed. The reply was, do you want this proved to you.

author: Epictetus
text: A certain young man, a rhetorician, came to see Epictetus, with his hair dressed more carefully than was usual and his attire in an ornamental style; whereupon Epictetus said, Tell me if you do not think that some dogs are beautiful and some horses, and so of all other animals.
plain: A young speaker arrived with extra neat hair and fancy clothes. He was asked if some dogs, horses, and other animals look lovely too.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, In what a man ought to be exercised who has made proficiency; and that we neglect the chief things
text: There are three things (topics,) in which a man ought to exercise himself who would be wise and good.
plain: There are three areas where a person must train if he wants to be wise and good.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, What is the matter on which a good man should be employed, and in what we ought chiefly to practise ourselves
text: The material for the wise and good man is his own ruling faculty: and the body is the material for the physician and the aliptes (the man who oils persons); the land is the matter for the husbandman.
plain: A wise and good person works with his own mind. A doctor works with the body, and a farmer works with the land.

author: Epictetus
text: When some person asked him how it happened that since reason has been more cultivated by the men of the present age, the progress made in former times was greater.
plain: Someone asked why reason is trained more now, while people in earlier times still got further.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To the administrator of the free cities who was an epicurean
text: As we exercise ourselves against sophistical questions, so we ought to exercise ourselves daily against appearances; for these appearances also propose questions to us.
plain: You drill against tricky questions, so drill each day against how things appear. Those appearances ask you questions as well.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To a certain rhetorician who was going up to rome on a suit
text: When a certain person came to him, who was going up to Rome on account of a suit which had regard to his rank, Epictetus inquired the reason of his going to Rome, and the man then asked what he thought about the matter.
plain: A man was going to the capital about a case on his rank. He was asked why, then he asked what the teacher thought.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, In what manner we ought to bear sickness
text: When the need of each opinion comes, we ought to have it in readiness: on the occasion of breakfast, such opinions as relate to breakfast; in the bath, those that concern the bath; in bed, those that concern bed.
plain: Keep the fitting thought ready for each moment. Think of breakfast at breakfast, of the bath in the bath, and of bed in bed.

author: Epictetus
text: We ought not to make our exercises consist in means contrary to nature and adapted to cause admiration, for if we do so, we who call ourselves philosophers, shall not differ at all from jugglers.
plain: Do not make your training a show of odd tricks meant to impress. If you do, you are no different from a street performer.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, What solitude is, and what kind of person a solitary man is
text: Solitude is a certain condition of a helpless man. For because a man is alone, he is not for that reason also solitary; just as though a man is among numbers, he is not therefore not solitary.
plain: Feeling cut off is the state of a helpless person. Being alone does not cause it, and a crowd does not end it.

author: Epictetus
text: As bad tragic actors cannot sing alone, but in company with many, so some persons cannot walk about alone.
plain: Poor actors in sad plays cannot sing by themselves, only beside a crowd. Some people cannot even walk around alone.

author: Epictetus
text: If a man, said Epictetus, opposes evident truths, it is not easy to find arguments by which we shall make him change his opinion.
plain: If someone pushes back on what is clearly true, finding words that change his mind is not easy.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, That we ought with caution to enter into familiar intercourse with men
text: If a man has frequent intercourse with others either for talk, or drinking together, or generally for social purposes, he must either become like them, or change them to his own fashion.
plain: If you often talk, drink, or hang out with people, you grow like them or they grow like you.

author: Epictetus
text: When one of his pupils inquired of Epictetus, and he was a person who appeared to be inclined to Cynicism, what kind of person a Cynic ought to be, and what was the notion of the thing, we will inquire, said Epictetus, at leisure; but I have so much to say to you that he who without God attempts so great a matter, is hateful to God, and has no other purpose than to act indecently in public.
plain: A student asked what a bold public challenger is like. Without God, such a person is hated by God and seeks only a shameful show.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, That we ought not to be moved by a desire of those things which are not in our power
text: Let not that which in another is contrary to nature be an evil to you; for you are not formed by nature to be depressed with others nor to be unhappy with others, but to be happy with them.
plain: Do not let what is unnatural in someone else become your harm. You are made to be happy with people, not sad along with them.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To those who fall off (desist) from their purpose
text: Consider as to the things which you proposed to yourself at first, which you have secured, and which you have not; and how you are pleased when you recall to memory the one, and are pained about the other; and if it is possible, recover the things wherein you failed.
plain: Check which early goals you kept and which you lost. You feel glad about one and hurt about the other, so recover what you can.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To those who fear want
text: Are you not ashamed at being more cowardly and more mean than fugitive slaves? How do they when they run away leave their masters? on what estates do they depend, and what domestics do they rely on?
plain: Are you not ashamed to be more scared and small than people who fled their masters. They left with no land and no helpers.

author: Epictetus
text: He is free who lives as he wishes to live; who is neither subject to compulsion nor to hindrance, nor to force; whose movements to action are not impeded, whose desires attain their purpose, and who does not fall into that which he would avoid.
plain: You are free when you live as you wish and nobody forces or blocks you. You get what you want and avoid what you dread.

author: Epictetus
text: To this matter before all you must attend, that you be never so closely connected with any of your former intimates or friends as to come down to the same acts as he does.
plain: Watch this before everything else. Never stay so close to an old friend that you drop into the same acts he does.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, What things we should exchange for other things
text: Keep this thought in readiness, when you lose anything external, what you acquire in place of it; and if it be worth more, never say, I have had a loss; neither if you have got a horse in place of an ass, or an ox in place of a sheep, nor a good action in place of a bit of money, nor in place of idle talk such tranquillity as befits a man, nor in place of lewd talk if you have acquired modesty.
plain: When an outside thing goes, notice what you gain instead. If the new thing is worth more, never call that a loss.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To those who are desirous of passing life in tranquillity
text: Remember that not only the desire of power and of riches makes us mean and subject to others, but even the desire of tranquillity, and of leisure, and of travelling abroad, and of learning.
plain: Wanting power and money can leave you petty and under others' control. So can wanting calm, free time, travel, or learning.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, Against the quarrelsome and ferocious
text: The wise and good man neither himself fights with any person, nor does he allow another, so far as he can prevent it.
plain: A wise and good person does not fight anybody. As far as he is able, he stops another person from fighting too.

author: Epictetus
text: From everything, which is or happens in the world, it is easy to praise Providence, if a man possesses these two qualities: the faculty of seeing what belongs and happens to all persons and things, and a grateful disposition.
plain: It is easy to give thanks for all that exists or happens. You need eyes for how everything fits, and a thankful spirit.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, Against those who lament over being pitied
text: I am grieved, a man says, at being pitied. Whether then is the fact of your being pitied a thing which concerns you or those who pity you?
plain: You say it hurts when people pity you. Does that pity belong to you, or to the people feeling it.

author: Epictetus
text: What makes the tyrant formidable? The guards, you say, and their swords, and the men of the bedchamber, and those who exclude them who would enter.
plain: What makes a harsh ruler scary. You point to the guards, their swords, the close servants, and people who block the door.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, To a person who had been changed to a character of shamelessness
text: When you see another man in the possession of power (magistracy), set against this the fact that you have not the want (desire) of power; when you see another rich, see what you possess in place of riches: for if you possess nothing in place of them, you are miserable; but if you have not the want of riches, know that you possess more than this man possesses and what is worth much more.
plain: If someone has power or money and you want none of it, you hold more. If you hold nothing in its place, you feel miserable.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, What things we ought to despise and what things we ought to value
text: The difficulties of all men are about external things, their helplessness is about external.
plain: People's troubles are about outside things. So is the helplessness they feel.

author: Epictetus
text: Some persons raise a question whether the social feeling is contained in the nature of man; and yet I think that these same persons would have no doubt that love of purity is certainly contained in it, and that if man is distinguished from other animals by anything, he is distinguished by this.
plain: Some ask if caring for others belongs in human nature. They never doubt that loving cleanliness does, and that this marks us off.

author: Epictetus
text: When you have remitted your attention for a short time, do not imagine this, that you will recover it when you choose; but let this thought be present to you, that in consequence of the fault committed today your affairs must be in a worse condition for all that follows.
plain: If your focus slips for a short while, do not expect it back whenever you like. That slip today leaves all later things worse.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, Against or to those who readily tell their own affairs
text: When a man has seemed to us to have talked with simplicity (candor) about his own affairs, how is it that at last we are ourselves also induced to discover to him our own secrets and we think this to be candid behavior?
plain: When someone talks openly about his own life, you end up telling your secrets. You treat that sharing as open behavior.

author: Epictetus
text: Before all other things then it is necessary to inquire about each of these opinions, whether it is affirmed truly or not truly.
plain: Before anything else, you need to test each of these beliefs. Ask whether each one is really true or not.

author: Epictetus
source: Discourses, How everything may be done acceptably to the gods
text: When some one asked, How may a man eat acceptably to the gods, he answered: If he can eat justly and contentedly, and with equanimity, and temperately, and orderly, will it not be also acceptable to the gods?
plain: Someone asked how a person can eat in a way the gods accept. Eat fairly, gladly, calmly, with restraint, and in good order.

author: Epictetus
text: Of things some are in our power, and others are not. In our power are opinion, movement towards a thing, desire, aversion, turning from a thing; and in a word, whatever are our acts.
plain: Some things are up to you and others are not. Yours are what you think, what you want, and what you choose to do.

author: Epictetus
text: On the occasion of every accident (event) that befalls you, remember to turn to yourself and inquire what power you have for turning it to use.
plain: Whenever something hits you, turn back to yourself and ask what strength you have for putting it to use.

author: Epictetus
text: Never say about anything, I have lost it, but say I have restored it. Is your child dead?
plain: Do not say you lost something. Say you gave it back, even in the case of a child who died.

author: Epictetus
text: If you intend to improve, throw away such thoughts as these: if I neglect my affairs, I shall not have the means of living: unless I chastise my slave, he will be bad.
plain: If you mean to improve, drop thoughts like these. I cannot live if I skip work, and my slave turns bad if I spare him.

author: Epictetus
text: If you would improve, submit to be considered without sense and foolish with respect to externals.
plain: If you want to get better, accept being seen as foolish about things outside you.

author: Epictetus
text: If you would have your children and your wife and your friends to live for ever, you are silly; for you would have the things which are not in your power to be in your power, and the things which belong to others to be yours.
plain: Wanting kids, a partner, and friends alive forever is a silly wish. Those lives are not yours to hold.

author: Epictetus
text: Remember that in life you ought to behave as at a banquet. Suppose that something is carried round and is opposite to you.
plain: In life, act the way you would at a big shared meal. Picture a dish coming around and stopping in front of you.

author: Epictetus
text: When you see a person weeping in sorrow either when a child goes abroad or when he is dead, or when the man has lost his property, take care that the appearance do not hurry you away with it, as if he were suffering in external things.
plain: When someone cries over a leaving child, a death, or lost money, do not get pulled along. The hurt is not in those outside things.

author: Epictetus
text: Remember that thou art an actor in a play, of such a kind as the teacher (author) may choose; if short, of a short one; if long, of a long one: if he wishes you to act the part of a poor man, see that you act the part naturally; if the part of a lame man, of a magistrate, of a private person, (do the same). For this is your duty, to act well the part that is given to you; but to select the part, belongs to another.
plain: You play a role someone else assigns, short or long. Play it well, because choosing the role falls to someone else.

author: Epictetus
text: When a raven has croaked inauspiciously, let not the appearance hurry you away with it; but straightway make a distinction in your mind and say, None of these things is signified to me, but either to my poor body, or to my small property, or to my reputation, or to my children, or to my wife: but to me all significations are auspicious if I choose.
plain: A bad bird call need not rush you. It concerns body, goods, or family, and it can still mean well if you choose.

author: Epictetus
text: You can be invincible, if you enter into no contest in which it is not in your power to conquer.
plain: You can stay unbeatable if you enter no contest where winning is out of your hands.

author: Epictetus
text: Remember that desire contains in it the profession (hope) of obtaining that which you desire; and the profession (hope) in aversion (turning from a thing) is that you will not fall into that which you attempt to avoid; and he who fails in his desire is unfortunate; and he who falls into that which he would avoid is unhappy.
plain: Wanting means you hope to get it, and avoiding means you hope to miss it. Fail either hope, and you end up hurt.

author: Epictetus
text: Remember that it is not he who reviles you or strikes you, who insults you, but it is your opinion about these things as being insulting. When then a man irritates you, you must know that it is your own opinion which has irritated you. Therefore especially try not to be carried away by the appearance. For if you once gain time and delay, you will more easily master yourself.
plain: A harsh word or blow does not insult you by itself. Your own view does, so a short pause lets you master yourself.

author: Epictetus
text: Let death and exile and every other thing which appears dreadful be daily before your eyes; but most of all death: and you will never think of anything mean nor will you desire anything extravagantly.
plain: Keep death, exile, and other scary things in mind each day, death most of all. Then petty thoughts and huge wants fade.

author: Epictetus
text: If you desire philosophy, prepare yourself from the beginning to be ridiculed, to expect that many will sneer at you, and say, He has all at once returned to us as a philosopher; and whence does he get this supercilious look for us?
plain: If you want this way of living, expect people to laugh from the start. They will say you came back looking down on them.

author: Epictetus
text: If it should ever happen to you to be turned to externals in order to please some person, you must know that you have lost your purpose in life. Be satisfied then in everything with being a philosopher; and if you wish to seem also to any person to be a philosopher, appear so to yourself, and you will be able to do this.
plain: If you turn outward just to please someone, you lose your aim. Seem right to yourself, and you can live that way.

author: Epictetus
text: Let not these thoughts afflict you, I shall live unhonored and be nobody nowhere.
plain: Do not let this thought eat at you, that you will live with no honor and be a nobody nowhere.

author: Epictetus
text: Has any man been preferred before you at a banquet, or in being saluted, or in being invited to a consultation?
plain: Was anyone placed ahead of you at a meal, a greeting, or an invite to a meeting.

author: Epictetus
text: We may learn the wish (will) of nature from the things in which we do not differ from one another: for instance, when your neighbor’s slave has broken his cup, or anything else, we are ready to say forthwith, that it is one of the things which happen.
plain: You see what is natural where people already agree. A servant breaks a neighbor's cup, and everyone says that kind of thing happens.

author: Epictetus
text: As a mark is not set up for the purpose of missing the aim, so neither does the nature of evil exist in the world.
plain: A target is not set out so people will miss it. Bad does not have a real place in the world either.

author: Epictetus
text: If any person was intending to put your body in the power of any man whom you fell in with on the way, you would be vexed; but that you put your understanding in the power of any man whom you meet, so that if he should revile you, it is disturbed and troubled, are you not ashamed at this?
plain: You would hate a stranger on the road controlling your body. Feel shame if a harsh word from him can shake your mind.

author: Epictetus
text: In every act observe the things which come first, and those which follow it; and so proceed to the act.
plain: With every action, look at what comes before it and what follows after. Then move ahead into the action.

author: Epictetus
text: In everything which pleases the soul, or supplies a want, or is loved, remember to add this to the (description, notion): What is the nature of each thing, beginning from the smallest?
plain: When something pleases your mind, fills a need, or is loved, add one question. Ask what it really is, beginning at the smallest bit.

author: Epictetus
text: Duties are universally measured by relations. Is a man a father? The precept is to take care of him, to yield to him in all things, to submit when he is reproachful, when he inflicts blows.
plain: What you owe people is set by how you are tied to them. A father gets care, yielding, and patience when he scolds or hits.

author: Epictetus
text: As to piety towards the gods you must know that this is the chief thing, to have right opinions about them, to think that they exist, and that they administer the All well and justly; and you must fix yourself in this principle (duty), to obey them, and to yield to them in everything which happens, and voluntarily to follow it as being accomplished by the wisest intelligence.
plain: Respect for the gods starts with right beliefs. They are real, they guide all things fairly, and you willingly follow what comes.

author: Epictetus
text: When you have recourse to divination, remember that you do not know how it will turn out, but that you are come to inquire from the diviner.
plain: When you go to ask about signs, remember the ending is still unknown. You came only to ask the person who reads them.

author: Epictetus
text: Immediately prescribe some character and some form to yourself, which you shall observe both when you are alone and when you meet with men.
plain: Right away, choose how you will carry yourself. Hold that same way in private and also around other people.

author: Epictetus
text: If you have received the impression of any pleasure, guard yourself against being carried away by it; but let the thing wait for you, and allow yourself a certain delay on your own part.
plain: If pleasure hits you hard, do not let it carry you away. Let the thing wait, and give yourself a short delay.

author: Epictetus
text: When you have decided that a thing ought to be done, and are doing it, never avoid being seen doing it, though the many shall form an unfavorable opinion about it. For if it is not right to do it, avoid doing the thing; but if it is right, why are you afraid of those who shall find fault wrongly?
plain: Once you are doing what you chose, never hide it. Skip it if wrong, and if it is right, ignore unfair blame.

author: Epictetus
text: As the proposition, it is either day, or it is night, is of great importance for the disjunctive argument, but for the conjunctive, is of no value, so in a symposium (entertainment) to select the larger share is of great value for the body, but for the maintenance of the social feeling is worth nothing.
plain: Day or night matters for one kind of proof, not another. The bigger share at a party helps the body, not the friendship.

author: Epictetus
text: If you have assumed a character above your strength, you have both acted in this manner in an unbecoming way, and you have neglected that which you might have fulfilled.
plain: If your role is above your strength, you act in a clumsy way and skip what you could finish.

author: Epictetus
text: In walking about, as you take care not to step on a nail, or to sprain your foot, so take care not to damage your own ruling faculty; and if we observe this rule in every act, we shall undertake this act with more security.
plain: While walking you avoid a nail and a twisted foot. Guard your mind the same way, so every act feels safer.

author: Epictetus
text: The measure of possession (property) is to every man the body, as the foot is of the shoe.
plain: Your body sets how much stuff is enough. It works like your foot setting the size of a shoe.

author: Epictetus
text: When you are going to take in hand any act remind yourself what kind of an act it is.
plain: Before you begin any action, pause and name what sort of action it really is.

author: Epictetus
text: Women forthwith from the age of fourteen are called by the men mistresses (, dominæ).
plain: Once girls reach fourteen, men already start calling them ladies.

author: Epictetus
text: It is a mark of a mean capacity to spend much time on the things which concern the body, such as much exercise, much eating, much drinking, much easing of the body, much copulation. But these things should be done as subordinate things; and let all your care be directed to the mind.
plain: Too much time on food, drink, exercise, and sex shows a small mind. Keep those as lesser things, and point your care at your mind.

author: Epictetus
text: When any person treats you ill or speaks ill of you, remember that he does this or says this because he thinks that it is his duty.
plain: When a person treats you badly or speaks badly of you, remember he thinks that doing so is right.

author: Epictetus
text: Everything has two handles, the one by which it may be borne, the other by which it may not. If your brother acts unjustly, do not lay hold of the act by that handle wherein he acts unjustly, for this is the handle which cannot be borne; but lay hold of the other, that he is your brother, that he was nurtured with you, and you will lay hold of the thing by that handle by which it can be borne.
plain: Each thing has a bearable handle and one you cannot carry. If your brother is unfair, hold on because you grew up together.

author: Epictetus
text: These reasonings do not cohere: I am richer than you, therefore I am better than you; I am more eloquent than you, therefore I am better than you. On the contrary, these rather cohere: I am richer than you, therefore my possessions are greater than yours; I am more eloquent than you, therefore my speech is superior to yours. But you are neither possession nor speech.
plain: Having more money or smoother speech does not make you better. Your things and your words are greater, but you are not those things.

author: Epictetus
text: Does a man bathe quickly (early)? do not say that he bathes badly, but that he bathes quickly. Does a man drink much wine? do not say that he does this badly, but say that he drinks much. For before you shall have determined the opinion how do you know whether he is acting wrong? Thus it will not happen to you to comprehend some appearances which are capable of being comprehended, but to assent to others.
plain: If someone washes fast, call it fast, not bad. If they drink a lot, say only that, until you know it is wrong.

author: Epictetus
text: On no occasion call yourself a philosopher, and do not speak much among the uninstructed about theorems (philosophical rules, precepts); but do that which follows from them.
plain: Do not give yourself a wise person's title, or lecture people who are new. Do what the lessons lead you to do.

author: Epictetus
text: When at a small cost you are supplied with everything for the body, do not be proud of this; nor, if you drink water, say on every occasion, I drink water.
plain: When cheap simple things cover your body's needs, do not brag. If you drink water, you do not have to announce it.

author: Epictetus
text: The condition and characteristic of an uninstructed person is this: he never expects from himself profit (advantage) nor harm, but from externals.
plain: Someone still learning looks for gain and harm from outside things, never from himself.

author: Epictetus
text: When a man is proud because he can understand and explain the writings of Chrysippus, say to yourself, If Chrysippus had not written obscurely, this man would have had nothing to be proud of.
plain: If a man brags that he can explain a murky writer, tell yourself the pride needs that murky writing.

author: Epictetus
text: Men are disturbed not by the things which happen, but by the opinions about the things; for example, death is nothing terrible, for if it were it would have seemed so to Socrates; for the opinion about death that it is terrible, is the terrible thing.
plain: You get shaken by your view of things, not by the things. The scary part of death is the view that it is scary.

author: Epictetus
text: Whatever things (rules) are proposed to you (for the conduct of life) abide by them, as if they were laws, as if you would be guilty of impiety if you transgressed any of them.
plain: Treat the rules given for your life like laws you would not break. Crossing one would feel like a deep wrong.

author: Epictetus
text: The first and most necessary place (part,) in philosophy is the use of theorems (precepts,), for instance, that we must not lie; the second part is that of demonstrations, for instance, How is it proved that we ought not to lie?
plain: The first need is using the rules, such as do not lie. Next comes showing how we know that rule is right.

author: Epictetus
text: In every thing (circumstance) we should hold these maxims ready to hand: Lead me, O Zeus, and thou O Destiny, The way that I am bid by you to go: To follow I am ready.
plain: Keep this ready in every case: lead me the way you ask, and I am ready to follow.

author: Epictetus
text: Be not elated at any advantage (excellence) which belongs to another. If a horse when he is elated should say, I am beautiful, one might endure it.
plain: Do not swell up over some gift that belongs to another. A horse may fairly boast that it looks lovely.

author: Epictetus
text: As on a voyage when the vessel has reached a port, if you go out to get water it is an amusement by the way to pick up a shellfish or some bulb, but your thoughts ought to be directed to the ship, and you ought to be constantly watching if the captain should call, and then you must throw away all those things, that you may not be bound and pitched into the ship like sheep.
plain: Small finds ashore are only a side pleasure. When the captain calls, drop them or you get tossed aboard like sheep.

author: Epictetus
text: Seek not that the things which happen should happen as you wish; but wish the things which happen to be as they are, and you will have a tranquil flow of life.
plain: Do not ask that events happen as you wish. Wish events to be as they already are, and life will flow calmly.

author: Epictetus
text: Disease is an impediment to the body, but not to the will, unless the will itself chooses. Lameness is an impediment to the leg, but not to the will. And add this reflection on the occasion of everything that happens; for you will find it an impediment to something else, but not to yourself.
plain: Sickness blocks your body, not your choice, unless you let it. A hurt leg blocks the leg, and other things block something else, not you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of my grandfather Verus I have learned to be gentle and meek, and to refrain from all anger and passion.
plain: I learned gentleness from my grandfather Verus, and how to hold back anger and strong feeling.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of Catulus, not to contemn any friend's expostulation, though unjust, but to strive to reduce him to his former disposition: freely and heartily to speak well of all my masters upon any occasion, as it is reported of Domitius, and Athenodotus: and to love my children with true affection.
plain: Do not dismiss a friend's complaint, even an unfair one, and help him soften. Speak well of your teachers, and love your kids truly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From my brother Severus, to be kind and loving to all them of my house and family; by whom also I came to the knowledge of Thrasea and Helvidius, and Cato, and Dio, and Brutus.
plain: From my brother Severus I learned kindness at home. Through him I came to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From Claudius Maximus, in all things to endeavour to have power of myself, and in nothing to be carried about; to be cheerful and courageous in all sudden chances and accidents, as in sicknesses: to love mildness, and moderation, and gravity: and to do my business, whatsoever it be, thoroughly, and without querulousness.
plain: From Maximus I learned to stay my own master, cheerful in sudden illness. Be calm and serious, and finish the work without griping.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In my father, I observed his meekness; his constancy without wavering in those things, which after a due examination and deliberation, he had determined.
plain: In my father I saw gentleness, and a steady hold on what he chose after careful thought.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Betimes in the morning say to thyself, This day I shalt have to do with an idle curious man, with an unthankful man, a railer, a crafty, false, or an envious man; an unsociable uncharitable man.
plain: Early each morning, tell yourself today you will meet someone idle, nosy, thankless, harsh, false, or jealous.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever I am, is either flesh, or life, or that which we commonly call the mistress and overruling part of man; reason.
plain: Whatever you are is body, or life, or the ruling part we usually call reason.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever proceeds from the gods immediately, that any man will grant totally depends from their divine providence.
plain: Anything that comes straight from the gods, people will agree, hangs completely on their divine care.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of him that brought me up, not to be fondly addicted to either of the two great factions of the coursers in the circus, called Prasini, and Veneti: nor in the amphitheatre partially to favour any of the gladiators, or fencers, as either the Parmularii, or the Secutores.
plain: From the man who raised me, I learned not to cling to a racing side. I also learned not to back one kind of fighter.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of Diognetus, not to busy myself about vain things, and not easily to believe those things, which are commonly spoken, by such as take upon them to work wonders, and by sorcerers, or prestidigitators, and impostors; concerning the power of charms, and their driving out of demons, or evil spirits; and the like.
plain: From Diognetus I learned to leave empty things alone. Do not quickly trust wonder talk, charms, or claims of driving spirits out.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To Rusticus I am beholding, that I first entered into the conceit that my life wanted some redress and cure.
plain: I owe Rusticus for this: I first got the idea that my life needed some mending and care.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From Alexander the Grammarian, to be un-reprovable myself, and not reproachfully to reprehend any man for a barbarism, or a solecism, or any false pronunciation, but dextrously by way of answer, or testimony, or confirmation of the same matter (taking no notice of the word) to utter it as it should have been spoken; or by some other such close and indirect admonition, handsomely and civilly to tell him of it.
plain: From Alexander I learned to keep my own words clean, and not scold a speech slip. Slip the right form into your reply, kindly.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of Fronto, to how much envy and fraud and hypocrisy the state of a tyrannous king is subject unto, and how they who are commonly called εὐπατρίδαι, _i.e._ nobly born, are in some sort incapable, or void of natural affection.
plain: From Fronto I learned how much envy, fraud, and false show surround a cruel ruler. People called high born can lack real affection.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of Alexander the Platonic, not often nor without great necessity to say, or to write to any man in a letter, 'I am not at leisure'; nor in this manner still to put off those duties, which we owe to our friends and acquaintances (to every one in his kind) under pretence of urgent affairs.
plain: From the other Alexander I learned not to say I have no time. Do not dodge friends by claiming the work is too pressing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: O my soul, the time I trust will be, when thou shalt be good, simple, single, more open and visible, than that body by which it is enclosed.
plain: Mind, I trust a time will come when you are good and simple. You will be more open than the body around you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As the spider, when it hath caught the fly that it hunted after, is not little proud, nor meanly conceited of herself: as he likewise that hath caught an hare, or hath taken a fish with his net: as another for the taking of a boar, and another of a bear: so may they be proud, and applaud themselves for their valiant acts against the Sarmatai, or northern nations lately defeated.
plain: A spider is proud of a caught fly, and a hunter of his catch. People may cheer the same way after beating a far nation.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To find out, and set to thyself some certain way and method of contemplation, whereby thou mayest clearly discern and represent unto thyself, the mutual change of all things, the one into the other. Bear it in thy mind evermore, and see that thou be throughly well exercised in this particular. For there is not anything more effectual to beget true magnanimity.
plain: Set yourself a way to picture how all things change into one another. Practice that often, because nothing builds a great heart better.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He hath got loose from the bonds of his body, and perceiving that within a very little while he must of necessity bid the world farewell, and leave all these things behind him, he wholly applied himself, as to righteousness in all his actions, so to the common nature in all things that should happen unto him.
plain: He has slipped the ties of his body and knows he must soon say goodbye. He turns to right acts, and to meeting whatever comes.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What use is there of suspicion at all? or, why should thoughts of mistrust, and suspicion concerning that which is future, trouble thy mind at all?
plain: Suspicion helps nothing. Doubt about what is coming should not bother your mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is that that is slow, and yet quick? merry, and yet grave? He that in all things doth follow reason for his guide.
plain: Slow and also quick, glad and also serious: that is the person who lets reason lead in everything.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the morning as soon as thou art awaked, when thy judgment, before either thy affections, or external objects have wrought upon it, is yet most free and impartial: put this question to thyself, whether if that which is right and just be done, the doing of it by thyself, or by others when thou art not able thyself; be a thing material or no.
plain: Each morning, your judgment is freest before feelings touch it. Ask if it matters who does right when you cannot.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Give what thou wilt, and take away what thou wilt, saith he that is well taught and truly modest, to Him that gives, and takes away. And it is not out of a stout and peremptory resolution, that he saith it, but in mere love, and humble submission.
plain: A modest, well taught person says give or take what you wish. He says it from love and humble acceptance, not from hard pride.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: So live as indifferent to the world and all worldly objects, as one who liveth by himself alone upon some desert hill.
plain: Live as unattached to the world and its things as if you lived alone on a bare hill.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Make it not any longer a matter of dispute or discourse, what are the signs and proprieties of a good man, but really and actually to be such.
plain: Do not keep arguing about what marks a good person. Become that person in real life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Ever to represent unto thyself; and to set before thee, both the general age and time of the world, and the whole substance of it.
plain: Always picture the full span of time, and the whole mass of the world in front of you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As one who is altogether governed by nature, let it be thy care to observe what it is that thy nature in general doth require.
plain: As someone led by nature, pay attention to what your nature, taken as a whole, is asking of you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Consider them through all actions and occupations, of their lives: as when they eat, and when they sleep: when they are in the act of necessary exoneration, and when in the act of lust.
plain: Look at people in ordinary moments of life, eating, sleeping, relieving themselves, and having sex.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That is best for every one, that the common nature of all doth send unto every one, and then is it best, when she doth send it.
plain: The best for each person is whatever nature sends them. It is best the moment it arrives.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The earth, saith the poet, doth often long after the rain. So is the glorious sky often as desirous to fall upon the earth, which argues a mutual kind of love between them.
plain: The poet says the earth often longs for rain. The bright sky longs to come down too, which shows a shared love.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either thou dost Continue in this kind of life and that is it, which so long thou hast been used unto and therefore tolerable: or thou doest retire, or leave the world, and that of thine own accord, and then thou hast thy mind: or thy life is cut off; and then mayst thou rejoice that thou hast ended thy charge.
plain: Stay, and habit makes this life bearable. Leave by choice and get your wish, or die glad that the duty is done.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that runs away from his master is a fugitive. But the law is every man's master.
plain: If you run from your master, you are a runaway. The law is every person's master.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From man is the seed, that once cast into the womb man hath no more to do with it.
plain: A man's seed starts the child. Once it enters the womb, that man has no further part in it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Ever to mind and consider with thyself; how all things that now are, have been heretofore much after the same sort, and after the same fashion that now they are: and so to think of those things which shall be hereafter also.
plain: Notice that today's things have shown up like this before. Think about later things in the same way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As a pig that cries and flings when his throat is cut, fancy to thyself every one to be, that grieves for any worldly thing and takes on.
plain: See each person who wails over some worldly thing as a pig that squeals and thrashes while being killed.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever it is that thou goest about, consider of it by thyself, and ask thyself, What? because I shall do this no more when I am dead, should therefore death seem grievous unto me?
plain: In whatever you are doing, ask yourself why death should feel bitter only because you will not do that again.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever doth happen unto thee, thou art naturally by thy natural constitution either able, or not able to bear.
plain: Whatever happens to you, you can bear it by nature, or you cannot.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou art offended with any man's transgression, presently reflect upon thyself; and consider what thou thyself art guilty of in the same kind.
plain: When another person's fault annoys you, turn at once to yourself and notice your own fault of that kind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou seest Satyro, think of Socraticus and Eutyches, or Hymen, and when Euphrates, think of Eutychio, and Sylvanus, when Alciphron, of Tropaeophorus, when Xenophon, of Crito, or Severus.
plain: When you see someone, think of another person like them. Keep doing that with each face you notice.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What a subject, and what a course of life is it, that thou doest so much desire to be rid of.
plain: What a life this is, the one you want so badly to get away from.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let it not be in any man's power, to say truly of thee, that thou art not truly simple, or sincere and open, or not good.
plain: Let nobody have the power to say, and be right, that you are not simple, sincere, open, or good.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As he that is bitten by a mad dog, is afraid of everything almost that he seeth: so unto him, whom the dogmata have once bitten, or in whom true knowledge hath made an impression, everything almost that he sees or reads be it never so short or ordinary, doth afford a good memento; to put him out of all grief and fear, as that of the poet, 'The winds blow upon the trees, and their leaves fall upon the ground.
plain: A mad dog's bite makes you fear nearly everything you see. Once true teaching bites, short ordinary things can lift your grief and fear.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A good eye must be good to see whatsoever is to be seen, and not green things only.
plain: A good eye has to see all that can be seen, and not only things that are green.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: There is not any man that is so happy in his death, but that some of those that are by him when he dies, will be ready to rejoice at his supposed calamity.
plain: Even a happy death leaves some people nearby glad about what they call a disaster.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Use thyself; as often, as thou seest any man do anything, presently (if it be possible) to say unto thyself, What is this man's end in this his action? But begin this course with thyself first of all, and diligently examine thyself concerning whatsoever thou doest.
plain: Each time you see a person do something, ask what aim they have. Begin that check with yourself and with all you do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember, that that which sets a man at work, and hath power over the affections to draw them either one way, or the other way, is not any external thing properly, but that which is hidden within every man's dogmata, and opinions: That, that is rhetoric; that is life; that (to speak true) is man himself.
plain: What puts you to work and tugs your feelings is a hidden opinion, not an outside thing. That opinion is the real you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Him that offends, to teach with love and meek ness, and to show him his error. But if thou canst not, then to blame thyself; or rather not thyself neither, if thy will and endeavours have not been wanting.
plain: Correct the person who slips, with love and gentleness, and show the mistake. If you cannot, blame yourself only if your effort fell short.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever it be that happens unto thee, it is that which from all time was appointed unto thee. For by the same coherence of causes, by which thy substance from all eternity was appointed to be, was also whatsoever should happen unto it, destinated and appointed.
plain: Whatever happens to you was assigned long ago. The same chain that made you also fixed what would happen to you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either with Epicurus, we must fondly imagine the atoms to be the cause of all things, or we must needs grant a nature.
plain: Either we foolishly imagine tiny atoms make everything, like Epicurus, or we accept that nature is real.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All parts of the world, (all things I mean that are contained within the whole world), must of necessity at some time or other come to corruption.
plain: Every piece of the world, meaning all that the world holds, must someday come apart.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Now that thou hast taken these names upon thee of good, modest, true; of ἔμφρων, σύμφρων, ὑπέρφρων; take heed lest at any times by doing anything that is contrary, thou be but improperly so called, and lose thy right to these appellations.
plain: You have taken the names good, modest, true, wise, and high minded. Do not act against them and lose your right to those names.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Toys and fooleries at home, wars abroad: sometimes terror, sometimes torpor, or stupid sloth: this is thy daily slavery.
plain: Play and nonsense at home, fighting far away, then fright, then heavy laziness. That pattern is your slavery each day.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The natural properties, and privileges of a reasonable soul are: That she seeth herself; that she can order, and compose herself: that she makes herself as she will herself: that she reaps her own fruits whatsoever, whereas plants, trees, unreasonable creatures, what fruit soever (be it either fruit properly, or analogically only) they bear, they bear them unto others, and not to themselves.
plain: A reasoning mind sees itself, shapes itself as it chooses, and keeps its fruit. Plants and animals give their fruit away.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The things themselves (which either to get or to avoid thou art put to so much trouble) come not unto thee themselves; but thou in a manner goest unto them. Let then thine own judgment and opinion concerning those things be at rest; and as for the things themselves, they stand still and quiet, without any noise or stir at all; and so shall all pursuing and flying cease.
plain: What you strain to grab or avoid does not come to you. You go to it, so quiet your mind and the chase can stop.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Then is the soul as Empedocles doth liken it, like unto a sphere or globe, when she is all of one form and figure: when she neither greedily stretcheth out herself unto anything, nor basely contracts herself, or lies flat and dejected; but shineth all with light, whereby she does see and behold the true nature, both that of the universe, and her own in particular.
plain: Your mind is like a smooth ball when it keeps one shape. It neither grabs nor slumps, and it shines on what is real.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Will any contemn me? let him look to that, upon what grounds he does it: my care shall be that I may never be found either doing or speaking anything that doth truly deserve contempt.
plain: If someone scorns you, let them check their reasons. Your care is to never do or say a thing that truly earns scorn.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: They contemn one another, and yet they seek to please one another: and whilest they seek to surpass one another in worldly pomp and greatness, they most debase and prostitute themselves in their better part one to another.
plain: They scorn each other and still try to win each other's favor. While chasing rank and show, they cheapen their better part.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How rotten and insincere is he, that saith, I am resolved to carry myself hereafter towards you with all ingenuity and simplicity.
plain: How hollow it is when a person says, later I will treat you with full honesty and plainness.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To live happily is an inward power of the soul, when she is affected with indifferency, towards those things that are by their nature indifferent.
plain: Happy living is an inner power of the mind. It is there when you stay easy about things that are neither good nor bad.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of everything thou must consider from whence it came, of what things it doth consist, and into what it will be changed: what will be the nature of it, or what it will be like unto when it is changed; and that it can suffer no hurt by this change.
plain: For each thing, ask where it came from, what is in it, and what it turns into. That change cannot harm it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What portion soever, either of air or fire there be in thee, although by nature it tend upwards, submitting nevertheless to the ordinance of the universe, it abides here below in this mixed body.
plain: Any bit of air or fire in you naturally wants to rise. It still stays down in your body, under the world's rule.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that hath not one and the self-same general end always as long as he liveth, cannot possibly be one and the self-same man always.
plain: Without one steady aim through your whole life, you cannot stay one and the same person.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A pleasant song or dance; the Pancratiast's exercise, sports that thou art wont to be much taken with, thou shalt easily contemn; if the harmonious voice thou shalt divide into so many particular sounds whereof it doth consist, and of every one in particular shall ask thyself; whether this or that sound is it, that doth so conquer thee.
plain: A favorite song, dance, or sport gets easy to drop if you split it up. Ask whether one small piece is what hooks you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember the fable of the country mouse and the city mouse, and the great fright and terror that this was put into.
plain: Remember the tale of the field mouse and the town mouse, and the great scare that followed.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The Lacedæmonians at their public spectacles were wont to appoint seats and forms for their strangers in the shadow, they themselves were content to sit anywhere.
plain: At their public shows, Spartans put visitors in the shade and were fine sitting any place themselves.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What Socrates answered unto Perdiccas, why he did not come unto him, Lest of all deaths I should die the worst kind of death, said he: that is, not able to requite the good that hath been done unto me.
plain: Socrates told Perdiccas he stayed away to avoid the worst death. That death is failing to repay good already done for him.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the ancient mystical letters of the Ephesians, there was an item, that a man should always have in his mind some one or other of the ancient worthies.
plain: Those old secret Ephesian writings said you should always keep some admired person from long ago in mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The Pythagoreans were wont betimes in the morning the first thing they did, to look up unto the heavens, to put themselves in mind of them who constantly and invariably did perform their task: as also to put themselves in mind of orderliness, or good order, and of purity, and of naked simplicity. For no star or planet hath any cover before it.
plain: Each morning Pythagoreans looked upward to remember steady work, order, purity, and bare simplicity. No star has anything covering it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How Socrates looked, when he was fain to gird himself with a skin, Xanthippe his wife having taken away his clothes, and carried them abroad with her, and what he said to his fellows and friends, who were ashamed; and out of respect to him, did retire themselves when they saw him thus decked.
plain: Picture Socrates wrapped in a skin after his wife took his clothes. His friends felt shame and backed away, but he still spoke to them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In matter of writing or reading thou must needs be taught before thou can do either: much more in matter of life. 'For thou art born a mere slave, to thy senses and brutish affections;' destitute without teaching of all true knowledge and sound reason.
plain: You must be taught before you can read or write, and life even more so. You begin ruled by your senses, without sound knowledge.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As they that long after figs in winter when they cannot be had; so are they that long after children, before they be granted them.
plain: People who want children before they are given are like people craving figs in winter, when none can be had.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That soul which is ever ready, even now presently (if need be) from the body, whether by way of extinction, or dispersion, or continuation in another place and estate to be separated, how blessed and happy is it!
plain: How peaceful is a mind ready now to leave the body. It may end, scatter, or go on in another place.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'As often as a father kisseth his child, he should say secretly with himself' (said Epictetus,) 'tomorrow perchance shall he die.' But these words be ominous.
plain: Whenever a father kisses his child, Epictetus said, he should quietly think the child might die tomorrow. Those words sound unlucky though.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'Of the free will there is no thief or robber:' out of Epictetus; Whose is this also: that we should find a certain art and method of assenting; and that we should always observe with great care and heed the inclinations of our minds, that they may always be with their due restraint and reservation, always charitable, and according to the true worth of every present object.
plain: Nobody can steal your free choice. Agree with care, and keep your mind kind, cautious, and fair to what is here.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Have I done anything charitably? then am I benefited by it. See that this upon all occasions may present itself unto thy mind, and never cease to think of it. What is thy profession? to be good. And how should this be well brought to pass, but by certain theorems and doctrines; some Concerning the nature of the universe, and some Concerning the proper and particular constitution of man?
plain: If you did something kind, you gained by it. Your work is to be good, by lessons on the world and on people.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How clearly doth it appear unto thee, that no other course of thy life could fit a true philosopher's practice better, than this very course, that thou art now already in?
plain: No other path fits a wise life better than the one you are already on.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A branch cut off from the continuity of that which was next unto it, must needs be cut off from the whole tree: so a man that is divided from another man, is divided from the whole society.
plain: A twig cut from the limb beside it is cut from the whole tree. Split from another person, and you are split from the group.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To grow together like fellow branches in matter of good correspondence and affection; but not in matter of opinions.
plain: Join like neighboring limbs in warmth and good feeling, but not by holding the same views.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is not possible that any nature should be inferior unto art, since that all arts imitate nature.
plain: Nature cannot be worse than a craft, since every craft copies nature.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever thou doest hereafter aspire unto, thou mayest even now enjoy and possess, if thou doest not envy thyself thine own happiness.
plain: What you aim at for later, you may already hold and enjoy, if you do not resent your own happiness.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How ridiculous and strange is he, that wonders at anything that happens in this life in the ordinary course of nature!
plain: How odd and silly someone looks who is shocked by anything that comes along in nature's normal way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either fate, (and that either an absolute necessity, and unavoidable decree; or a placable and flexible Providence) or all is a mere casual confusion, void of all order and government.
plain: Either fate rules, fixed tight or able to bend. Or else all is just a jumble, with no order at all.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: At the conceit and apprehension that such and such a one hath sinned, thus reason with thyself; What do I know whether this be a sin indeed, as it seems to be?
plain: When you think someone has done wrong, ask yourself what you know. Check if it really is wrong.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it be not fitting, do it not. If it be not true, speak it not. Ever maintain thine own purpose and resolution free from all compulsion and necessity.
plain: If it does not fit, leave it undone. If it is not true, leave it unsaid, and keep your aim free from being forced.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of everything that presents itself unto thee, to consider what the true nature of it is, and to unfold it, as it were, by dividing it into that which is formal: that which is material: the true use or end of it, and the just time that it is appointed to last.
plain: When something shows up, open it up. Separate its shape, its material, its real use, and how long it should last.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is high time for thee, to understand that there is somewhat in thee, better and more divine than either thy passions, or thy sensual appetites and affections.
plain: It is past time you saw this. Something in you is better and more godlike than your cravings and strong feelings.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember that all is but opinion, and all opinion depends of the mind. Take thine opinion away, and then as a ship that hath stricken in within the arms and mouth of the harbour, a present calm; all things safe and steady: a bay, not capable of any storms and tempests: as the poet hath it.
plain: Everything is only opinion, and opinion sits in the mind. Drop that, and you get calm, like a ship safe in harbor.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: No operation whatsoever it he, ceasing for a while, can be truly said to suffer any evil, because it is at an end.
plain: When something stops, even for a short time, it is not harmed, because it has ended.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: These three things thou must have always in a readiness: first concerning thine own actions, whether thou doest nothing either idly, or otherwise, than justice and equity do require: and concerning those things that happen unto thee externally, that either they happen unto thee by chance, or by providence; of which two to accuse either, is equally against reason.
plain: Check that you act fairly, not idly. Outside events come by chance or plan, so blaming either is senseless.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Cast away from thee opinion, and thou art safe. And what is it that hinders thee from casting of it away?
plain: Drop your opinion and you are safe. What stops you from letting it go.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: God beholds our minds and understandings, bare and naked from these material vessels, and outsides, and all earthly dross.
plain: God sees our minds and thoughts bare, without the body, the outside, and all the earthly junk.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let thy thoughts ever run upon them, who once for some one thing or other, were moved with extraordinary indignation; who were once in the highest pitch of either honour, or calamity; or mutual hatred and enmity; or of any other fortune or condition whatsoever.
plain: Keep in mind people once wildly angry, or at the peak of fame, disaster, or hatred. Any other condition belongs there too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To them that ask thee, Where hast thou seen the Gods, or how knowest thou certainly that there be Gods, that thou art so devout in their worship?
plain: People may ask where you have seen the gods. They also ask how you know they exist, since you honor them so much.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Herein doth consist happiness of life, for a man to know thoroughly the true nature of everything; what is the matter, and what is the form of it: with all his heart and soul, ever to do that which is just, and to speak the truth. What then remaineth but to enjoy thy life in a course and coherence of good actions, one upon another immediately succeeding, and never interrupted, though for never so little a while?
plain: A happy life means knowing what things really are, acting fairly, and telling the truth. Then enjoy one good action after another.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: There is but one light of the sun, though it be intercepted by walls and mountains, and other thousand objects.
plain: There is only one sunlight, even when walls, mountains, and a thousand other things block it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What doest thou desire? To live long. What? To enjoy the operations of a sensitive soul; or of the appetitive faculty? or wouldst thou grow, and then decrease again?
plain: Do you want a long life, or only to feel, want, grow, and then shrink.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What a small portion of vast and infinite eternity it is, that is allowed unto every one of us, and how soon it vanisheth into the general age of the world: of the common substance, and of the common soul also what a small portion is allotted unto us: and in what a little clod of the whole earth (as it were) it is that thou doest crawl.
plain: You get a tiny, fast-fading bit of endless time, shared matter, and shared mind. You crawl on a small lump of earth.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is the present estate of my understanding? For herein lieth all indeed. As for all other things, they are without the compass of mine own will: and if without the compass of my will, then are they as dead things unto me, and as it were mere smoke.
plain: What is your mind like right now? That is everything, because all else sits outside your choice and is dead, like smoke.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To stir up a man to the contempt of death this among other things, is of good power and efficacy, that even they who esteemed pleasure to be happiness, and pain misery, did nevertheless many of them contemn death as much as any.
plain: Even people who lived for pleasure still scorned death as much as anyone. That can help you scorn it too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I have often wondered how it should come to pass, that every man loving himself best, should more regard other men's opinions concerning himself than his own.
plain: I often wonder why you love yourself most, yet care more what others think of you than what you think.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: how come it to pass that the Gods having ordered all other things so well and so lovingly, should be overseen in this one only thing, that whereas then hath been some very good men that have made many covenants as it were with God and by many holy actions and outward services contracted a kind of familiarity with Him; that these men when once they are dead, should never be restored to life, but be extinct for ever.
plain: You may wonder why the gods ordered everything so lovingly, yet good people close to them die and stay gone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Use thyself even unto those things that thou doest at first despair of. For the left hand we see, which for the most part lieth idle because not used; yet doth it hold the bridle with more strength than the right, because it hath been used unto it.
plain: Practice the things you first think you cannot do. Your left hand sits idle, yet holds the reins harder because it was trained.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All worldly things thou must behold and consider, dividing them into matter, form, and reference, or their proper end.
plain: Look at everything in the world by splitting it into stuff, shape, and the purpose it serves.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How happy is man in this his power that hath been granted unto him: that he needs not do anything but what God shall approve, and that he may embrace contentedly, whatsoever God doth send unto him?
plain: You are lucky to have this gift. You need only do what God approves, and you can welcome whatever God sends.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever doth happen in the ordinary course and consequence of natural events, neither the Gods, (for it is not possible, that they either wittingly or unwittingly should do anything amiss) nor men, (for it is through ignorance, and therefore against their wills that they do anything amiss) must be accused. None then must be accused.
plain: Do not blame the gods or people for ordinary natural events. The gods cannot do wrong, and people slip only by not knowing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember how long thou hast already put off these things, and how often a certain day and hour as it were, having been set unto thee by the gods, thou hast neglected it.
plain: Remember how long you have already put this off, and how often you missed the hour the gods had set.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Consider with thyself how man, and by what part of his, is joined unto God, and how that part of man is affected, when it is said to be diffused.
plain: Think about which part of you joins you to God. Ask what that part is like when it is spread out.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou shouldst live three thousand, or as many as ten thousands of years, yet remember this, that man can part with no life properly, save with that little part of life, which he now lives: and that which he lives, is no other, than that which at every instant he parts with.
plain: Even if you lived thousands of years, you only leave the small life you have now. You give that bit up each moment.

author: Marcus Aurelius
