text: Remember that all is but opinion and conceit, for those things are plain and apparent, which were spoken unto Monimus the Cynic; and as plain and apparent is the use that may be made of those things, if that which is true and serious in them, be received as well as that which is sweet and pleasing.
plain: All of this is just opinion. What Monimus heard is clear, and useful if you accept the hard truth and the sweet part.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A man's soul doth wrong and disrespect itself first and especially, when as much as in itself lies it becomes an aposteme, and as it were an excrescency of the world, for to be grieved and displeased with anything that happens in the world, is direct apostacy from the nature of the universe; part of which, all particular natures of the world, are.
plain: Your mind hurts itself first when it pulls away from the world and gets upset by what happens. You are part of that same world.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The time of a man's life is as a point; the substance of it ever flowing, the sense obscure; and the whole composition of the body tending to corruption.
plain: Your life is a tiny point, its stuff always moving, your senses dim, and your whole body heading toward decay.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let it be thy earnest and incessant care as a Roman and a man to perform whatsoever it is that thou art about, with true and unfeigned gravity, natural affection, freedom and justice: and as for all other cares, and imaginations, how thou mayest ease thy mind of them.
plain: Work at what you are doing with care, warmth, freedom, and fairness, as a person should. Ease other worries and daydreams from your mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do, soul, do; abuse and contemn thyself; yet a while and the time for thee to respect thyself, will be at an end. Every man's happiness depends from himself, but behold thy life is almost at an end, whiles affording thyself no respect, thou dost make thy happiness to consist in the souls, and conceits of other men.
plain: Keep putting yourself down and the time to respect yourself will run out. Your happiness is yours, yet you place it in other people's minds.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Why should any of these things that happen externally, so much distract thee? Give thyself leisure to learn some good thing, and cease roving and wandering to and fro.
plain: Outside events do not need to pull you off course. Give yourself time to learn something good, and stop drifting around.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: These things thou must always have in mind: What is the nature of the universe, and what is mine--in particular: This unto that what relation it hath: what kind of part, of what kind of universe it is: And that there is nobody that can hinder thee, but that thou mayest always both do and speak those things which are agreeable to that nature, whereof thou art a part.
plain: Remember the world's nature, your nature, and how your part fits. Nobody can stop you from saying and doing what matches that nature.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Theophrastus, where he compares sin with sin (as after a vulgar sense such things I grant may be compared:) says well and like a philosopher, that those sins are greater which are committed through lust, than those which are committed through anger.
plain: Theophrastus said wrongs done from craving are worse than wrongs done from anger.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever thou dost affect, whatsoever thou dost project, so do, and so project all, as one who, for aught thou knowest, may at this very present depart out of this life.
plain: Do and plan everything as if you might leave this life at this very moment.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Consider how quickly all things are dissolved and resolved: the bodies and substances themselves, into the matter and substance of the world: and their memories into the general age and time of the world.
plain: Everything breaks down fast. Bodies return to the world's stuff, and memories fade into the world's long stretch of time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A man must not only consider how daily his life wasteth and decreaseth, but this also, that if he live long, he cannot be certain, whether his understanding shall continue so able and sufficient, for either discreet consideration, in matter of businesses; or for contemplation: it being the thing, whereon true knowledge of things both divine and human, doth depend.
plain: Each day your life shrinks, and long years may dull your mind for work or deep thought. Real knowing rests on that mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Use thine opinative faculty with all honour and respect, for in her indeed is all: that thy opinion do not beget in thy understanding anything contrary to either nature, or the proper constitution of a rational creature.
plain: Treat your power to judge with respect, because it is everything. Do not let a judgment fight your nature as a thinking person.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is this, that now my fancy is set upon? of what things doth it consist? how long can it last? which of all the virtues is the proper virtue for this present use? as whether meekness, fortitude, truth, faith, sincerity, contentation, or any of the rest?
plain: Ask what your mind is fixed on, what it is made of, and how long it lasts. Then ask which good quality fits this moment.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As physicians and chirurgeons have always their instruments ready at hand for all sudden cures; so have thou always thy dogmata in a readiness for the knowledge of things, both divine and human: and whatsoever thou dost, even in the smallest things that thou dost, thou must ever remember that mutual relation, and connection that is between these two things divine, and things human.
plain: Keep your guiding ideas ready, like a doctor keeps tools ready. In every small act, remember that human things and godly things are tied together.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be not deceived; for thou shalt never live to read thy moral commentaries, nor the acts of the famous Romans and Grecians; nor those excerpta from several books; all which thou hadst provided and laid up for thyself against thine old age. Hasten therefore to an end, and giving over all vain hopes, help thyself in time if thou carest for thyself, as thou oughtest to do.
plain: You will not get to read the notes you saved for old age. Drop empty hopes and help yourself now if you care.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To steal, to sow, to buy, to be at rest, to see what is to be done (which is not seen by the eyes, but by another kind of sight:) what these words mean, and how many ways to be understood, they do not understand. The body, the soul, the understanding. As the senses naturally belong to the body, and the desires and affections to the soul, so do the dogmata to the understanding.
plain: People miss what stealing, planting, buying, resting, and seeing what to do mean. The body has senses, the mind has wants, and thought has judgments.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To be capable of fancies and imaginations, is common to man and beast. To be violently drawn and moved by the lusts and desires of the soul, is proper to wild beasts and monsters, such as Phalaris and Nero were.
plain: Imagining things is common to people and animals. Being dragged by strong wants belongs to beasts and cruel people like Phalaris and Nero.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Hippocrates having cured many sicknesses, fell sick himself and died. The Chaldeans and Astrologians having foretold the deaths of divers, were afterwards themselves surprised by the fates.
plain: Hippocrates healed many illnesses, then got sick and died. The star-readers who predicted other deaths were later caught by fate themselves.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Spend not the remnant of thy days in thoughts and fancies concerning other men, when it is not in relation to some common good, when by it thou art hindered from some other better work.
plain: Do not fill your remaining days with thoughts about others unless they serve a shared good. Otherwise they block better work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do nothing against thy will, nor contrary to the community, nor without due examination, nor with reluctancy.
plain: Do nothing against your will, against the group, without a real look, or with a heavy heart.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To be cheerful, and to stand in no need, either of other men's help or attendance, or of that rest and tranquillity, which thou must be beholding to others for. Rather like one that is straight of himself, or hath ever been straight, than one that hath been rectified.
plain: Be cheerful without needing help or borrowed calm from others. Be like someone who was always upright, not later straightened.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Never esteem of anything as profitable, which shall ever constrain thee either to break thy faith, or to lose thy modesty; to hate any man, to suspect, to curse, to dissemble, to lust after anything, that requireth the secret of walls or veils.
plain: Never call something useful if it pushes you to break trust, drop shame, hate, or suspect. Cursing, faking, or craving a hidden thing counts too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the mind that is once truly disciplined and purged, thou canst not find anything, either foul or impure, or as it were festered: nothing that is either servile, or affected: no partial tie; no malicious averseness; nothing obnoxious; nothing concealed.
plain: In a mind that is truly trained and cleaned, you find nothing rotten, slavish, fake, one-sided, bitter, or hidden.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That inward mistress part of man if it be in its own true natural temper, is towards all worldly chances and events ever so disposed and affected, that it will easily turn and apply itself to that which may be, and is within its own power to compass, when that cannot be which at first it intended.
plain: When your inner guide is in its natural state, it can turn. It moves toward what you can still do if the first plan fails.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: These two rules, thou must have always in a readiness. First, do nothing at all, but what reason proceeding from that regal and supreme part, shall for the good and benefit of men, suggest unto thee.
plain: Keep this rule ready: do nothing except what your highest reason suggests for people's good.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Hast thou reason? I have. Why then makest thou not use of it? For if thy reason do her part, what more canst thou require?
plain: You have reason, so use it. If it does its job, there is nothing more you need.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As a part hitherto thou hast had a particular subsistence: and now shalt thou vanish away into the common substance of Him, who first begot thee, or rather thou shalt be resumed again into that original rational substance, out of which all others have issued, and are propagated. Many small pieces of frankincense are set upon the same altar, one drops first and is consumed, another after; and it comes all to one.
plain: You return to the shared source that made you. Incense bits on one altar burn at different times and end the same.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Within ten days, if so happen, thou shalt be esteemed a god of them, who now if thou shalt return to the dogmata and to the honouring of reason, will esteem of thee no better than of a mere brute, and of an ape.
plain: People who now call you a brute or an ape may call you a god in ten days. That happens if you return to reason.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not as though thou hadst thousands of years to live. Death hangs over thee: whilst yet thou livest, whilst thou mayest, be good.
plain: You do not have thousands of years. Death is close, so while you live and still can, be good.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Now much time and leisure doth he gain, who is not curious to know what his neighbour hath said, or hath done, or hath attempted, but only what he doth himself, that it may be just and holy? or to express it in Agathos' words, Not to look about upon the evil conditions of others, but to run on straight in the line, without any loose and extravagant agitation.
plain: You gain time by watching only whether your own actions are fair. Leave what a neighbor said or did, and run straight.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He who is greedy of credit and reputation after his death, doth not consider, that they themselves by whom he is remembered, shall soon after every one of them be dead; and they likewise that succeed those; until at last all memory, which hitherto by the succession of men admiring and soon after dying hath had its course, be quite extinct.
plain: If you crave credit after you die, remember this. The people who recall you will die too, and so will memory itself.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If so be that the souls remain after death (say they that will not believe it); how is the air from all eternity able to contain them?
plain: Some who doubt ask how the air could hold every mind forever, if minds stay on after death.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not to wander out of the way, but upon every motion and desire, to perform that which is just: and ever to be careful to attain to the true natural apprehension of every fancy, that presents itself.
plain: Do not drift off the path. On every urge, do what is fair, and see each thought for what it really is.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is expedient unto thee, O World, is expedient unto me; nothing can either be 'unseasonable unto me, or out of date, which unto thee is seasonable.
plain: Whatever is good for you, world, is good for me. Nothing that fits your timing can be badly timed for me.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let nothing be done rashly, and at random, but all things according to the most exact and perfect rules of art.
plain: Do not act in a rush or at random. Do everything by the exact rules of the craft.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: They will say commonly, Meddle not with many things, if thou wilt live cheerfully.
plain: People often say that if you want a cheerful life, do not poke into many things.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Try also how a good man's life; (of one, who is well pleased with those things whatsoever, which among the common changes and chances of this world fall to his own lot and share; and can live well contented and fully satisfied in the justice of his own proper present action, and in the goodness of his disposition for the future:) will agree with thee.
plain: Try a good person's life, pleased with whatever lands in your lot. Stay content with a fair action now and a good aim later.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either this world is a κόσμος or comely piece, because all disposed and governed by certain order: or if it be a mixture, though confused, yet still it is a comely piece.
plain: Either the world is a beautiful whole because order runs it. Or it is a mixed jumble and still beautiful.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: A black or malign disposition, an effeminate disposition; an hard inexorable disposition, a wild inhuman disposition, a sheepish disposition, a childish disposition; a blockish, a false, a scurril, a fraudulent, a tyrannical: what then? If he be a stranger in the world, that knows not the things that are in it; why not be a stranger as well, that wonders at the things that are done in it?
plain: So what if people are cruel, false, or childish. If ignorance makes you a stranger, be one who wonders at what they do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He is a true fugitive, that flies from reason, by which men are sociable. He blind, who cannot see with the eyes of his understanding.
plain: You are truly on the run if you flee the reason that lets people live together. You are blind if your understanding cannot see.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: There is, who without so much as a coat; and there is, who without so much as a book, doth put philosophy in practice. I am half naked, neither have I bread to eat, and yet I depart not from reason, saith one. But I say; I want the food of good teaching, and instructions, and yet I depart not from reason.
plain: Some people keep to reason with no coat, no book, no bread. You can lack good teaching and still not leave reason.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What art and profession soever thou hast learned, endeavour to affect it, and comfort thyself in it; and pass the remainder of thy life as one who from his whole heart commits himself and whatsoever belongs unto him, unto the gods: and as for men, carry not thyself either tyrannically or servilely towards any.
plain: Love and take comfort in the skill you learned. Give your whole self to the gods, and neither boss people nor bow.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Those words which once were common and ordinary, are now become obscure and obsolete; and so the names of men once commonly known and famous, are now become in a manner obscure and obsolete names.
plain: Words that were once everyday are now unclear and unused. Names that were once famous have faded the same way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is now present, and from day to day hath its existence; all objects of memories, and the minds and memories themselves, incessantly consider, all things that are, have their being by change and alteration.
plain: Look at what is here each day, and at memories and minds. Everything that exists does so by changing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: They seek for themselves private retiring places, as country villages, the sea-shore, mountains; yea thou thyself art wont to long much after such places.
plain: People look for quiet hideaways, like country villages, the shore, and mountains, and you often long for those places too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou art now ready to die, and yet hast thou not attained to that perfect simplicity: thou art yet subject to many troubles and perturbations; not yet free from all fear and suspicion of external accidents; nor yet either so meekly disposed towards all men, as thou shouldest; or so affected as one, whose only study and only wisdom is, to be just in all his actions.
plain: You could die now, yet you stay troubled, fearful, and far from simple. You are not gentle, or set only on fair actions.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Behold and observe, what is the state of their rational part; and those that the world doth account wise, see what things they fly and are afraid of; and what things they hunt after.
plain: Look at how people think, and at what the so-called wise run from and chase.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In another man's mind and understanding thy evil Cannot subsist, nor in any proper temper or distemper of the natural constitution of thy body, which is but as it were the coat or cottage of thy soul.
plain: Your harm cannot live in someone else's mind. It also cannot live in your body, which is only a coat around your mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Ever consider and think upon the world as being but one living substance, and having but one soul, and how all things in the world, are terminated into one sensitive power; and are done by one general motion as it were, and deliberation of that one soul; and how all things that are, concur in the cause of one another's being, and by what manner of connection and concatenation all things happen.
plain: See the world as one living thing with one mind. Everything shares one sense, one motion, and one linked cause.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What art thou, that better and divine part excepted, but as Epictetus said well, a wretched soul, appointed to carry a carcass up and down?
plain: Apart from your better, higher part, you are a poor mind. Epictetus said you are meant to carry a dead body around.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To suffer change can be no hurt; as no benefit it is, by change to attain to being. The age and time of the world is as it were a flood and swift current, consisting of the things that are brought to pass in the world. For as soon as anything hath appeared, and is passed away, another succeeds, and that also will presently out of sight.
plain: Change does not hurt, and coming to be by change is no gain. The world is a fast flood where each thing appears, then vanishes.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, is, in the course of nature, as usual and ordinary as a rose in the spring, and fruit in summer.
plain: What happens here is as normal in nature as roses during spring, or fruit during summer.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let that of Heraclitus never be out of thy mind, that the death of earth, is water, and the death of water, is air; and the death of air, is fire; and so on the contrary.
plain: Keep Heraclitus in mind: earth dies into water, water into air, air into fire, and then the other way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Even as if any of the gods should tell thee, Thou shalt certainly die to-morrow, or next day, thou wouldst not, except thou wert extremely base and pusillanimous, take it for a great benefit, rather to die the next day after, than to-morrow; (for alas, what is the difference!) so, for the same reason, think it no great matter to die rather many years after, than the very next day.
plain: Only a coward would prize dying a day later over tomorrow. So dying many years later is no big deal either.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let it be thy perpetual meditation, how many physicians who once looked so grim, and so theatrically shrunk their brows upon their patients, are dead and gone themselves.
plain: Keep noticing how many grim doctors who frowned hard at their patients are now dead and gone themselves.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If to understand and to be reasonable be common unto all men, then is that reason, for which we are termed reasonable, common unto all.
plain: If understanding and being reasonable belong to all people, then the reason we are called reasonable belongs to everyone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must be like a promontory of the sea, against which though the waves beat continually, yet it both itself stands, and about it are those swelling waves stilled and quieted.
plain: Be like a rocky point in the sea. Waves keep hitting it, yet it stands, and the water around it grows calm.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Oh, wretched I, to whom this mischance is happened! nay, happy I, to whom this thing being happened, I can continue without grief; neither wounded by that which is present, nor in fear of that which is to come.
plain: Don't say poor me, say lucky me. You can go on without grief, unhurt now and not scared of what comes.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is but an ordinary coarse one, yet it is a good effectual remedy against the fear of death, for a man to consider in his mind the examples of such, who greedily and covetously (as it were) did for a long time enjoy their lives.
plain: A plain help against fearing death is to picture people who clung to life and enjoyed it for years.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let thy course ever be the most compendious way. The most compendious, is that which is according to nature: that is, in all both words and deeds, ever to follow that which is most sound and perfect. For such a resolution will free a man from all trouble, strife, dissembling, and ostentation.
plain: Take the short path that follows nature in your words and actions. It frees you from trouble, fighting, faking, and showing off.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As generation is, so also death, a secret of nature's wisdom: a mixture of elements, resolved into the same elements again, a thing surely which no man ought to be ashamed of: in a series of other fatal events and consequences, which a rational creature is subject unto, not improper or incongruous, nor contrary to the natural and proper constitution of man himself.
plain: Death, like birth, undoes a mix and sends the parts back. A thinking person has no reason to feel shame about that.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Such and such things, from such and such causes, must of necessity proceed. He that would not have such things to happen, is as he that would have the fig-tree grow without any sap or moisture. In sum, remember this, that within a very little while, both thou and he shall both be dead, and after a little while more, not so much as your names and memories shall be remaining.
plain: Wanting these things not to happen is like wanting a fig tree with no sap. Soon you and he will both be dead, then forgotten.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let opinion be taken away, and no man will think himself wronged. If no man shall think himself wronged, then is there no more any such thing as wrong. That which makes not man himself the worse, cannot make his life the worse, neither can it hurt him either inwardly or outwardly. It was expedient in nature that it should be so, and therefore necessary.
plain: Drop your opinion and nobody feels wronged, so no wrong remains. What does not make you worse cannot hurt you, as nature required.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever doth happen in the world, doth happen justly, and so if thou dost well take heed, thou shalt find it.
plain: Whatever happens in the world happens fairly, and if you look closely you will see that.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Conceit no such things, as he that wrongeth thee conceiveth, or would have thee to conceive, but look into the matter itself, and see what it is in very truth.
plain: Skip the story the person who hurt you wants you to believe. Look at the thing itself and see the truth.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the morning when thou findest thyself unwilling to rise, consider with thyself presently, it is to go about a man's work that I am stirred up.
plain: When you do not want to get up, remember you are rising for the work a human should do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must comfort thyself in the expectation of thy natural dissolution, and in the meantime not grieve at the delay; but rest contented in those two things.
plain: Take comfort in expecting your natural end, and do not grieve that it is delayed. Rest content with those two things.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is the use that now at this present I make of my soul? Thus from time to time and upon all occasions thou must put this question to thyself; what is now that part of mine which they call the rational mistress part, employed about? Whose soul do I now properly possess? a child's? or a youth's? a woman's? or a tyrant's? some brute, or some wild beast's soul?
plain: Ask whose mind you have right now. It could be a child's, a youth's, a woman's, a tyrant's, or an animal's.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What those things are in themselves, which by the greatest part are esteemed good, thou mayest gather even from this.
plain: You can tell what the things most people call good really are on their own.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All that I consist of, is either form or matter. No corruption can reduce either of these unto nothing: for neither did I of nothing become a subsistent creature.
plain: You are only shape and stuff. Rot cannot turn either into nothing, because you did not come from nothing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Reason, and rational power, are faculties which content themselves with themselves, and their own proper operations.
plain: Reason and the power to think are happy with themselves and with the work they do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Such as thy thoughts and ordinary cogitations are, such will thy mind be in time.
plain: Your everyday thoughts become the kind of mind you will have over time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To desire things impossible is the part of a mad man. But it is a thing impossible, that wicked man should not commit some such things.
plain: Wanting the impossible is what a mad person does. A bad person is bound to do some bad things.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: After one consideration, man is nearest unto us; as we are bound to do them good, and to bear with them.
plain: From one view, other people are nearest to us. We are tied to helping them and putting up with them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Honour that which is chiefest and most powerful in the world, and that is it, which makes use of all things, and governs all things. So also in thyself; honour that which is chiefest, and most powerful; and is of one kind and nature with that which we now spake of. For it is the very same, which being in thee, turneth all other things to its own use, and by whom also thy life is governed.
plain: Honor the strongest thing in the world, the one that uses and guides everything. Honor that same power in you, because it guides your life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which doth not hurt the city itself; cannot hurt any citizen. This rule thou must remember to apply and make use of upon every conceit and apprehension of wrong.
plain: What does not hurt the city cannot hurt a citizen. Remember to use this rule whenever you feel wronged.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How easy a thing is it for a man to put off from him all turbulent adventitious imaginations, and presently to be in perfect rest and tranquillity!
plain: It is easy to drop the stormy thoughts that were never yours and be fully calm at once.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let not that chief commanding part of thy soul be ever subject to any variation through any corporal either pain or pleasure, neither suffer it to be mixed with these, but let it both circumscribe itself, and confine those affections to their own proper parts and members.
plain: Keep your guiding mind steady through pain or pleasure in the body. Leave those feelings in the parts where they belong.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To live with the Gods. He liveth with the Gods, who at all times affords unto them the spectacle of a soul, both contented and well pleased with whatsoever is afforded, or allotted unto her; and performing whatsoever is pleasing to that Spirit, whom (being part of himself) Jove hath appointed to every man as his overseer and governor.
plain: Living with the gods means you stay glad about whatever you get, and you do what your inner guide wants.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be not angry neither with him whose breath, neither with him whose arm holes, are offensive.
plain: Do not get mad at someone just because their breath or armpits smell bad.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'Where there shall neither roarer be, nor harlot.' Why so? As thou dost purpose to live, when thou hast retired thyself to some such place, where neither roarer nor harlot is: so mayest thou here.
plain: You plan to live somewhere without rowdy people or prostitutes. You can live that way right here.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That rational essence by which the universe is governed, is for community and society; and therefore hath it both made the things that are worse, for the best, and hath allied and knit together those which are best, as it were in an harmony.
plain: The mind running the world wants people together. It uses lesser things for the good and joins the best as one.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How hast thou carried thyself hitherto towards the Gods? towards thy parents? towards thy brethren? towards thy wife? towards thy children? towards thy masters? thy foster-fathers? thy friends? thy domestics? thy servants?
plain: Ask how you have treated God, your parents, your siblings, your partner, your kids, your teachers, and people at home.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Why should imprudent unlearned souls trouble that which is both learned, and prudent? And which is that that is so? she that understandeth the beginning and the end, and hath the true knowledge of that rational essence, that passeth through all things subsisting, and through all ages being ever the same, disposing and dispensing as it were this universe by certain periods of time.
plain: An untaught mind has no business troubling the one that sees the start, the end, and what guides every age.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Within a very little while, thou wilt be either ashes, or a sceletum; and a name perchance; and perchance, not so much as a name.
plain: Soon you will be ashes or bones. Maybe a name stays, or maybe even that is gone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou mayest always speed, if thou wilt but make choice of the right way; if in the course both of thine opinions and actions, thou wilt observe a true method.
plain: You can always do well if you pick the right path. Keep your thoughts and actions on a true plan.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If this neither be my wicked act, nor an act anyways depending from any wickedness of mine, and that by it the public is not hurt; what doth it concern me?
plain: If this is not your bad act and the group is not hurt, it does not concern you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Think thyself fit and worthy to speak, or to do anything that is according to nature, and let not the reproach, or report of some that may ensue upon it, ever deter thee.
plain: See yourself as fit to say or do what fits your nature. Do not let blame or gossip stop you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let death surprise me when it will, and where it will, I may be εὔμοιρος, or a happy man, nevertheless. For he is a happy man, who in his lifetime dealeth unto himself a happy lot and portion. A happy lot and portion is, good inclinations of the soul, good desires, good actions.
plain: Let death come whenever and wherever it wants. You stay glad if your mindset, wishes, and actions are good.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I continue my course by actions according to nature, until I fall and cease, breathing out my last breath into that air, by which continually breathed in I did live; and falling upon that earth, out of whose gifts and fruits my father gathered his seed, my mother her blood, and my nurse her milk, out of which for so many years I have been provided, both of meat and drink.
plain: You keep acting in a natural way until your last breath. Then you return to the air and the ground that fed you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: No man can admire thee for thy sharp acute language, such is thy natural disability that way.
plain: Nobody can praise you for sharp clever talk. That skill just is not in you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Such there be, who when they have done a good turn to any, are ready to set them on the score for it, and to require retaliation.
plain: Some people do a kind thing and then keep score. They expect you to pay them back.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The form of the Athenians' prayer did run thus: 'O rain, rain, good Jupiter, upon all the grounds and fields that belong to the Athenians.' Either we should not pray at all, or thus absolutely and freely; and not every one for himself in particular alone.
plain: Their old prayer asked rain for every field, not one person's farm. Either pray for everyone, or do not pray at all.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As we say commonly, The physician hath prescribed unto this man, riding; unto another, cold baths; unto a third, to go barefoot: so it is alike to say, The nature of the universe hath prescribed unto this man sickness, or blindness, or some loss, or damage or some such thing.
plain: A doctor may order riding, cold baths, or bare feet for someone. In the same way, life may hand you sickness, blindness, or loss.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The matter itself, of which the universe doth consist, is of itself very tractable and pliable. That rational essence that doth govern it, hath in itself no cause to do evil. It hath no evil in itself; neither can it do anything that is evil: neither can anything be hurt by it. And all things are done and determined according to its will and prescript.
plain: The stuff of the world is soft and easy to shape. The mind that guides it holds no harm and hurts nothing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it were that thou hadst at one time both a stepmother, and a natural mother living, thou wouldst honour and respect her also; nevertheless to thine own natural mother would thy refuge, and recourse be continually.
plain: If you had a step mum and a birth mum, you would respect both. You would still go back to your own mum.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How marvellous useful it is for a man to represent unto himself meats, and all such things that are for the mouth, under a right apprehension and imagination! as for example: This is the carcass of a fish; this of a bird; and this of a hog.
plain: It helps to see food as it really is. That plate is a dead fish, a dead bird, or a dead pig.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Those things which the common sort of people do admire, are most of them such things as are very general, and may be comprehended under things merely natural, or naturally affected and qualified: as stones, wood, figs, vines, olives.
plain: Most things people look up to are plain and natural. Think stones, wood, figs, vines, and olives.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Some things hasten to be, and others to be no more. And even whatsoever now is, some part thereof hath already perished.
plain: Some things rush to exist, and others rush to end. Even what is here now has already partly gone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Under, above, and about, are the motions of the elements; but the motion of virtue, is none of those motions, but is somewhat more excellent and divine. Whose way (to speed and prosper in it) must be through a way, that is not easily comprehended.
plain: Things move down, up, and around. Right living is a higher kind of movement, and the way into it is hard to see.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Who can choose but wonder at them? They will not speak well of them that are at the same time with them, and live with them; yet they themselves are very ambitious, that they that shall follow, whom they have never seen, nor shall ever see, should speak well of them. As if a man should grieve that he hath not been commended by them, that lived before him.
plain: They will not praise people living with them now. Still they want people they will never meet to praise them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Do not ever conceive anything impossible to man, which by thee cannot, or not without much difficulty be effected; but whatsoever in general thou canst Conceive possible and proper unto any man, think that very possible unto thee also.
plain: Do not call a thing impossible just because it is hard for you. If any person can do it, you can too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Suppose that at the palestra somebody hath all to-torn thee with his nails, and hath broken thy head.
plain: Picture this at training: someone scratches you up with their nails and breaks your head.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Be it all one unto thee, whether half frozen or well warm; whether only slumbering, or after a full sleep; whether discommended or commended thou do thy duty: or whether dying or doing somewhat else; for that also 'to die,' must among the rest be reckoned as one of the duties and actions of our lives.
plain: Cold or warm, tired or rested, blamed or praised, you can still do your part. Dying counts as one of life's tasks too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If anybody shall reprove me, and shall make it apparent unto me, that in any either opinion or action of mine I do err, I will most gladly retract. For it is the truth that I seek after, by which I am sure that never any man was hurt; and as sure, that he is hurt that continueth in any error, or ignorance whatsoever.
plain: If someone shows you that a belief or action is wrong, take it back gladly. Truth never hurts you, but staying wrong does.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: I for my part will do what belongs unto me; as for other things, whether things unsensible or things irrational; or if rational, yet deceived and ignorant of the true way, they shall not trouble or distract me.
plain: You will do what is yours to do. Other things, even confused people, will not throw you off.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Alexander of Macedon, and he that dressed his mules, when once dead both came to one.
plain: Alexander and the man who cared for his mules ended up the same once they were dead.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: if any should put this question unto thee, how this word Antoninus is written, wouldst thou not presently fix thine intention upon it, and utter out in order every letter of it?
plain: If someone asked how the name Antoninus is spelled, you would focus and say each letter in order.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Is it not a cruel thing to forbid men to affect those things, which they conceive to agree best with their own natures, and to tend most to their own proper good and behoof?
plain: It is cruel to stop people from wanting what they believe fits their own nature and their own good.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Death is a cessation from the impression of the senses, the tyranny of the passions, the errors of the mind, and the servitude of the body.
plain: Death is a rest from what your senses feel, from strong feelings, from mind mistakes, and from your body's bonds.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If in this kind of life thy body be able to hold out, it is a shame that thy soul should faint first, and give over, take heed, lest of a philosopher thou become a mere Cæsar in time, and receive a new tincture from the court.
plain: If your body can last, shame on a mind that quits first. Do not become a mere ruler shaped by the court.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Stir up thy mind, and recall thy wits again from thy natural dreams, and visions, and when thou art perfectly awoken, and canst perceive that they were but dreams that troubled thee, as one newly awakened out of another kind of sleep look upon these worldly things with the same mind as thou didst upon those, that thou sawest in thy sleep.
plain: Wake your mind up from its everyday dreams. Once you see they were only dreams, look at daily things the same way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Look in, let not either the proper quality, or the true worth of anything pass thee, before thou hast fully apprehended it.
plain: Look closely. Do not miss what something really is or what it is worth before you fully get it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As long as the foot doth that which belongeth unto it to do, and the hand that which belongs unto it, their labour, whatsoever it be, is not unnatural.
plain: As long as your foot and your hand do their own jobs, the work is natural, whatever it is.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Asia, Europe; what are they, but as corners of the whole world; of which the whole sea, is but as one drop; and the great Mount Athos, but as a clod, as all present time is but as one point of eternity.
plain: Asia and Europe are small corners of the world. The sea is a drop, the mountain a clod, and now a point in forever.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Fit and accommodate thyself to that estate and to those occurrences, which by the destinies have been annexed unto thee; and love those men whom thy fate it is to live with; but love them truly.
plain: Settle into the life and events that landed with you. Love the people you live with, and love them for real.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: We all work to one effect, some willingly, and with a rational apprehension of what we do: others without any such knowledge.
plain: You all work toward one result. Some do it on purpose and understand it, others do it without knowing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If so be that the Gods have deliberated in particular of those things that should happen unto me, I must stand to their deliberation, as discrete and wise.
plain: If God has carefully decided what happens to you, accept that decision as a wise one.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All substances come soon to their change, and either they shall be resolved by way of exhalation (if so be that all things shall be reunited into one substance), or as others maintain, they shall be scattered and dispersed.
plain: Everything soon changes. It either fades back into one stuff, or it breaks apart and spreads out.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever in any kind doth happen to any one, is expedient to the whole. And thus much to content us might suffice, that it is expedient for the whole in general.
plain: Whatever happens to any one person helps the whole. Knowing it helps the whole can be enough for you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As the ordinary shows of the theatre and of other such places, when thou art presented with them, affect thee; as the same things still seen, and in the same fashion, make the sight ingrateful and tedious; so must all the things that we see all our life long affect us. For all things, above and below, are still the same, and from the same causes. When then will there be an end?
plain: Shows get dull when the same things repeat the same way. Life stays like that, from the same causes, so you ask when it ends.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let the several deaths of men of all sorts, and of all sorts of professions, and of all sort of nations, be a perpetual object of thy thoughts,... so that thou mayst even come down to Philistio, Phœbus, and Origanion.
plain: Keep thinking about the deaths of every kind of person, job, and nation. Include even the names nobody remembers.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou wilt comfort and cheer thyself, call to mind the several gifts and virtues of them, whom thou dost daily converse with; as for example, the industry of the one; the modesty of another; the liberality of a third; of another some other thing.
plain: When you want comfort, remember the good traits of people you see each day. One works hard, another is modest, another is generous.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Dost thou grieve that thou dost weigh but so many pounds, and not three hundred rather? Just as much reason hast thou to grieve that thou must live but so many years, and not longer. For as for bulk and substance thou dost content thyself with that proportion of it that is allotted unto thee, so shouldst thou for time.
plain: You do not grieve that you weigh this much and not far more. You have the same reason to accept your years.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let us do our best endeavours to persuade them; but however, if reason and justice lead thee to it, do it, though they be never so much against it.
plain: Try your best to persuade them. If clear reason and fairness lead you there, do it even if they fight it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The ambitious supposeth another man's act, praise and applause, to be his own happiness; the voluptuous his own sense and feeling; but he that is wise, his own action.
plain: The fame chaser treats someone else's praise as their joy. The pleasure chaser trusts feelings, and the wise one trusts their own action.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is in thy power absolutely to exclude all manner of conceit and opinion, as concerning this matter; and by the same means, to exclude all grief and sorrow from thy soul. For as for the things and objects themselves, they of themselves have no such power, whereby to beget and force upon us any opinion at all.
plain: You can shut out every opinion about this, and shut grief out of your mind too. Things themselves cannot force a view on you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Use thyself when any man speaks unto thee, so to hearken unto him, as that in the interim thou give not way to any other thoughts; that so thou mayst (as far as is possible) seem fixed and fastened to his very soul, whosoever he be that speaks unto thee.
plain: When someone speaks to you, listen so hard that other thoughts stay out. Let them feel you are right there with them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Will either passengers, or patients, find fault and complain, either the one if they be well carried, or the others if well cured? Do they take care for any more than this; the one, that their shipmaster may bring them safe to land, and the other, that their physician may effect their recovery?
plain: Passengers do not complain if carried well, nor patients if healed well. They only want a safe landing or a real recovery.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How many of them who came into the world at the same time when I did, are already gone out of it?
plain: How many people born when you were have already left this life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To them that are sick of the jaundice, honey seems bitter; and to them that are bitten by a mad dog, the water terrible; and to children, a little ball seems a fine thing. And why then should I be angry? or do I think that error and false opinion is less powerful to make men transgress, than either choler, being immoderate and excessive, to cause the jaundice; or poison, to cause rage?
plain: Honey tastes bitter to the sick, and a child prizes a little ball. Wrong ideas push people just as strongly, so anger is useless.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: No man can hinder thee to live as thy nature doth require. Nothing can happen unto thee, but what the common good of nature doth require.
plain: Nobody can stop you from living the way your nature asks. Nothing can happen to you except what nature's common good asks.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What manner of men they be whom they seek to please, and what to get, and by what actions: how soon time will cover and bury all things, and how many it hath already buried!
plain: See who they try to please, what they want, and how they chase it. Time soon buries it all, and has buried so much already.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let this be thy only joy, and thy only comfort, from one sociable kind action without intermission to pass unto another, God being ever in thy mind.
plain: Let your only joy be moving from one kind act to the next without a stop. Keep God in your mind the whole time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The rational commanding part, as it alone can stir up and turn itself; so it maketh both itself to be, and everything that happeneth, to appear unto itself, as it will itself.
plain: The guiding part of you can turn itself. It makes itself, and everything that happens, look the way it chooses.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: According to the nature of the universe all things particular are determined, not according to any other nature, either about compassing and containing; or within, dispersed and contained; or without, depending.
plain: Each thing is set by the whole world's nature. Nothing around it, inside it, or outside it decides it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whensoever by some present hard occurrences thou art constrained to be in some sort troubled and vexed, return unto thyself as soon as may be, and be not out of tune longer than thou must needs. For so shalt thou be the better able to keep thy part another time, and to maintain the harmony, if thou dost use thyself to this continually; once out, presently to have recourse unto it, and to begin again.
plain: When hard events shake you, come back to yourself quickly and do not stay off key. Practice starting again so you can keep your part.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is wickedness? It is that which many time and often thou hast already seen and known in the world.
plain: What is badness? It is something you have met many times before and already know from life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As several members in one body united, so are reasonable creatures in a body divided and dispersed, all made and prepared for one common operation.
plain: Like parts of one body, thinking people are spread out but made for one shared job.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of things that are external, happen what will to that which can suffer by external accidents. Those things that suffer let them complain themselves, if they will; as for me, as long as I conceive no such thing, that that which is happened is evil, I have no hurt; and it is in my power not to conceive any such thing.
plain: Let outside events hit whatever they can hurt. You stay unharmed if you do not call what happened bad.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, thou must be good; not for any man's sake, but for thine own nature's sake; as if either gold, or the emerald, or purple, should ever be saying to themselves, Whatsoever any man either doth or saith, I must still be an emerald, and I must keep my colour.
plain: No matter what anyone does or says, stay good for your own nature. Like a gem, you keep your color.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This may ever be my comfort and security: my understanding, that ruleth over all, will not of itself bring trouble and vexation upon itself.
plain: Here is a steady comfort: your understanding, which is in charge, will not bring trouble on itself.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What is εὐδαιμονία, or happiness: but ἀγαθὸς δαίμων, or, a good dæmon, or spirit?
plain: Happiness is nothing other than a good spirit with you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Is any man so foolish as to fear change, to which all things that once were not owe their being?
plain: Would you be so silly as to fear change, when change is why things that once were nothing now exist.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Through the substance of the universe, as through a torrent pass all particular bodies, being all of the same nature, and all joint workers with the universe itself as in one of our bodies so many members among themselves.
plain: Bodies pass through the stuff of the world like a flood. They share one nature and work together like limbs.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The nature of the universe, of the common substance of all things as it were of so much wax hath now perchance formed a horse; and then, destroying that figure, hath new tempered and fashioned the matter of it into the form and substance of a tree: then that again into the form and substance of a man: and then that again into some other.
plain: Nature shapes the shared stuff of things like wax. It forms a horse, then a tree, then a person, then something else.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: An angry countenance is much against nature, and it is oftentimes the proper countenance of them that are at the point of death.
plain: An angry face goes against nature. It is often the face of someone close to death.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whensoever any man doth trespass against other, presently consider with thyself what it was that he did suppose to be good, what to be evil, when he did trespass.
plain: When someone wrongs another person, ask what they thought was good and what they thought was bad right then.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What fear is there that thy dogmata, or philosophical resolutions and conclusions, should become dead in thee, and lose their proper power and efficacy to make thee live happy, as long as those proper and correlative fancies, and representations of things on which they mutually depend (which continually to stir up and revive is in thy power,) are still kept fresh and alive?
plain: Do not fear your settled views will die and stop helping you live well. You can keep the pictures they depend on fresh.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Fancy not to thyself things future, as though they were present but of those that are present, take some aside, that thou takest most benefit of, and consider of them particularly, how wonderfully thou wouldst want them, if they were not present.
plain: Do not picture future things as if they are already here. Notice how you would miss the present things that help you most.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Wipe off all opinion stay the force and violence of unreasonable lusts and affections: circumscribe the present time examine whatsoever it be that is happened, either to thyself or to another: divide all present objects, either in that which is formal or material think of the last hour.
plain: Drop opinions, hold back wild wants, and stay inside this moment. Take what happened apart, and remember your last hour.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All things (saith he) are by certain order and appointment. And what if the elements only.
plain: He says all things follow a set order and plan. He even asks whether that is true of the elements alone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Out of Plato. 'He then whose mind is endowed with true magnanimity, who hath accustomed himself to the contemplation both of all times, and of all things in general; can this mortal life (thinkest thou) seem any great matter unto him?
plain: From Plato: a truly big mind looks at all times and all things. Ask if this short life can seem huge to that mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Out of Antisthenes. 'It is a princely thing to do well, and to be ill-spoken of.
plain: From Antisthenes: doing well while people speak badly of you is a royal thing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Out of several poets and comics. 'It will but little avail thee, to turn thine anger and indignation upon the things themselves that have fallen across unto thee.
plain: From the poets: it helps very little to aim your anger at the things themselves that got in your way.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Out of Plato. 'My answer, full of justice and equity, should be this: Thy speech is not right, O man! if thou supposest that he that is of any worth at all, should apprehend either life or death, as a matter of great hazard and danger; and should not make this rather his only care, to examine his own actions, whether just or unjust: whether actions of a good, or of a wicked man, &c.
plain: From Plato: a worthy person does not see life or death as huge danger. They only check if their actions are fair or not.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To look back upon things of former ages, as upon the manifold changes and conversions of several monarchies and commonwealths.
plain: Look back on earlier ages as the many changes and turnovers of kingdoms and states.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He hath a stronger body, and is a better wrestler than I. What then? Is he more bountiful? is he more modest? Doth he bear all adverse chances with more equanimity: or with his neighbour's offences with more meekness and gentleness than I?
plain: He has a stronger body and wrestles better than you. Ask if he is kinder, more modest, or calmer with setbacks and others' faults.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Where the matter may be effected agreeably to that reason, which both unto the Gods and men is common, there can be no just cause of grief or sorrow.
plain: Where a thing can follow the reason shared by God and people, there is no fair cause for grief.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which most men would think themselves most happy for, and would prefer before all things, if the Gods would grant it unto them after their deaths, thou mayst whilst thou livest grant unto thyself; to live again.
plain: What people would want most after death is to live again. You can give yourself that while you are still alive.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Look not about upon other men's minds and understandings; but look right on forwards whither nature, both that of the universe, in those things that happen unto thee; and thine in particular, in those things that are done by thee: doth lead, and direct thee.
plain: Do not look around at other people's minds. Look forward where nature leads, both in what happens to you and in what you do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As one who had lived, and were now to die by right, whatsoever is yet remaining, bestow that wholly as a gracious overplus upon a virtuous life.
plain: You have lived, and you could rightly die now. Treat the time left as a bonus for living well.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must use thyself also to keep thy body fixed and steady; free from all loose fluctuant either motion, or posture. And as upon thy face and looks, thy mind hath easily power over them to keep them to that which is grave and decent; so let it challenge the same power over the whole body also. But so observe all things in this kind, as that it be without any manner of affectation.
plain: Keep your body steady, not loose. As your mind keeps your face decent, let it do that for your whole body, with no show.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The art of true living in this world is more like a wrestler's, than a dancer's practice. For in this they both agree, to teach a man whatsoever falls upon him, that he may be ready for it, and that nothing may cast him down.
plain: Real living is more like wrestling than dancing. It trains you to be ready for whatever lands on you, so nothing knocks you down.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must continually ponder and consider with thyself, what manner of men they be, and for their minds and understandings what is their present estate, whose good word and testimony thou dost desire.
plain: Always think about what kind of people they are, and where their minds are, when you want their good word.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What pain soever thou art in, let this presently come to thy mind, that it is not a thing whereof thou needest to be ashamed, neither is it a thing whereby thy understanding, that hath the government of all, can be made worse.
plain: Whatever pain you are in, remember it is nothing to be ashamed of. It cannot make your understanding, which runs things, any worse.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Take heed lest at any time thou stand so affected, though towards unnatural evil men, as ordinary men are commonly one towards another.
plain: Watch that you do not feel about bad people the way ordinary people usually feel about each other.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How know we whether Socrates were so eminent indeed, and of so extraordinary a disposition?
plain: Ask how we know whether Socrates was really that outstanding or truly unusual in character.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: For it is a thing very possible, that a man should be a very divine man, and yet be altogether unknown.
plain: It is very possible for a person to be truly godly and still be completely unknown.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Free from all compulsion in all cheerfulness and alacrity thou mayst run out thy time, though men should exclaim against thee never so much, and the wild beasts should pull in sunder the poor members of thy pampered mass of flesh.
plain: You can finish your time free and cheerful, even if people shout against you. Even if wild beasts tear your body apart.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Word after word, every one by itself, must the things that are spoken be conceived and understood; and so the things that are done, purpose after purpose, every one by itself likewise.
plain: Take spoken things word by word, each one on its own. Take actions the same way, one aim after another, each on its own.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Then hath a man attained to the estate of perfection in his life and conversation, when he so spends every day, as if it were his last day: never hot and vehement in his affections, nor yet so cold and stupid as one that had no sense; and free from all manner of dissimulation.
plain: You live fully when you treat each day as your last. Stay neither too heated nor numb, and do not pretend.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Can the Gods, who are immortal, for the continuance of so many ages bear without indignation with such and so many sinners, as have ever been, yea not only so, but also take such care for them, that they want nothing; and dust thou so grievously take on, as one that could bear with them no longer; thou that art but for a moment of time? yea thou that art one of those sinners thyself?
plain: God bears wrongdoers for ages and cares that they lack nothing. You last a moment, are one of them, and still cannot bear them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What object soever, our reasonable and sociable faculty doth meet with, that affords nothing either for the satisfaction of reason, or for the practice of charity, she worthily doth think unworthy of herself.
plain: If something gives nothing to reason or kindness, your friendly mind rightly finds it unworthy.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou hast done well, and another is benefited by thy action, must thou like a very fool look for a third thing besides, as that it may appear unto others also that thou hast done well, or that thou mayest in time, receive one good turn for another?
plain: When you do well and someone benefits, do not foolishly chase praise or payback.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The nature of the universe did once certainly before it was created, whatsoever it hath done since, deliberate and so resolve upon the creation of the world.
plain: Before the world was made, the nature of the whole surely thought it through and decided to create it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let not things future trouble thee. For if necessity so require that they come to pass, thou shalt (whensoever that is) be provided for them with the same reason, by which whatsoever is now present, is made both tolerable and acceptable unto thee.
plain: Do not let future things trouble you. If they must happen, the same reason that makes today bearable will meet them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is material, doth soon vanish away into the common substance of the whole; and whatsoever is formal, or, whatsoever doth animate that which is material, is soon resumed into the common reason of the whole; and the fame and memory of anything, is soon swallowed up by the general age and duration of the whole.
plain: Stuff soon fades into the shared mass. Form and life return to the shared mind, and fame is soon swallowed by time.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To a reasonable creature, the same action is both according to nature, and according to reason.
plain: For a thinking person, the same action fits both nature and reason.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This also, among other things, may serve to keep thee from vainglory; if thou shalt consider, that thou art now altogether incapable of the commendation of one, who all his life long, or from his youth at least, hath lived a philosopher's life.
plain: You cannot take the praise of someone who has thought well since youth. That can keep pride away.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This, what is it in itself, and by itself, according to its proper constitution? What is the substance of it? What is the matter, or proper use? What is the form or efficient cause? What is it for in this world, and how long will it abide? Thus must thou examine all things, that present themselves unto thee.
plain: Ask what a thing is, what it is made of, what it is for, and how long it lasts.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When thou art hard to be stirred up and awaked out of thy sleep, admonish thyself and call to mind, that, to perform actions tending to the common good is that which thine own proper constitution, and that which the nature of man do require. But to sleep, is common to unreasonable creatures also. And what more proper and natural, yea what more kind and pleasing, than that which is according to nature?
plain: When getting up feels hard, remember that helping people is your nature. Sleep is shared with animals, while living your nature feels better.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As every fancy and imagination presents itself unto thee, consider (if it be possible) the true nature, and the proper qualities of it, and reason with thyself about it.
plain: When a thought shows up, look at what it really is and talk it through with yourself.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: At thy first encounter with any one, say presently to thyself: This man, what are his opinions concerning that which is good or evil? as concerning pain, pleasure, and the causes of both; concerning honour, and dishonour, concerning life and death? thus and thus.
plain: When you first meet someone, ask yourself what they call good or bad, pain or pleasure, life or death.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember, that to change thy mind upon occasion, and to follow him that is able to rectify thee, is equally ingenuous, as to find out at the first, what is right and just, without help. For of thee nothing is required, ti, is beyond the extent of thine own deliberation and jun. merit, and of thine own understanding.
plain: Letting someone correct you is as honest as finding what is right on your own. You are only asked what your mind can do.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If it were thine act and in thine own power, wouldest thou do it? If it were not, whom dost tin accuse? the atoms, or the Gods? For to do either, the part of a mad man. Thou must therefore blame nobody, but if it be in thy power, redress what is amiss; if it be not, to what end is it to complain? For nothing should be done but to some certain end.
plain: Blame nobody, not atoms or gods. If you can fix what is wrong, do it, and skip complaints that have no purpose.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever dieth and falleth, however and wheresoever it die and fall, it cannot fall out of the world, here it have its abode and change, here also shall it have its dissolution into its proper elements. The same are the world's elements, and the elements of which thou dost consist. And they when they are changed, they murmur not; why shouldest thou?
plain: Whatever dies stays here and turns into the same parts you are made from. Those parts do not complain, and neither should you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whatsoever is, was made for something: as a horse, a vine. Why wonderest thou? The sun itself will say of itself, I was made for something; and so hath every god its proper function. What then were then made for? to disport and delight thyself? See how even common sense and reason cannot brook it.
plain: Everything exists for a purpose, even the sun. Common sense cannot accept that you were made only to play.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Nature hath its end as well in the end and final consummation of anything that is, as in the begin-nine and continuation of it.
plain: Nature has a purpose in how things end, just as it does in how they start and keep going.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As one that tosseth up a ball. And what is a ball the better, if the motion of it be upwards; or the worse if it be downwards; or if it chance to fall upon the ground?
plain: A ball is no better for going up, and no worse for falling down to the ground.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Upon every action that thou art about, put this question to thyself; How will this when it is done agree with me?
plain: Before each thing you do, ask whether it will still fit you once it is done.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which must be the subject of thy consideration, is either the matter itself, or the dogma, or the operation, or the true sense and signification.
plain: What you need to look at is the thing itself, the belief, the action, or the real meaning.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Most justly have these things happened unto thee: why dost not thou amend? O but thou hadst rather become good to-morrow, than to be so to-day.
plain: These things happened to you fairly, so why wait to change. You would rather be better tomorrow than today.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Shall I do it? I will; so the end of my action be to do good unto men. Doth anything by way of cross or adversity happen unto me? I accept it, with reference unto the Gods, and their providence; the fountain of all things, from which whatsoever comes to pass, doth hang and depend.
plain: I will act when the aim is to help people. If something hard comes, I accept it as coming from the gods.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: By one action judge of the rest: this bathing which usually takes up so much of our time, what is it? Oil, sweat, filth; or the sordes of the body: an excrementitious viscosity, the excrements of oil and other ointments used about the body, and mixed with the sordes of the body: all base and loathsome. And such almost is every part of our life; and every worldly object.
plain: Judge the rest of life by a bath: oil, sweat, and dirt. Almost every part of life is that low and foul.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Lucilla buried Verus; then was Lucilla herself buried by others. So Secunda Maximus, then Secunda herself.
plain: Lucilla buried Verus, then others buried Lucilla. Secunda buried Maximus, then others buried Secunda too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The true joy of a man, is to do that which properly belongs unto a man. That which is most proper unto a man, is, first, to be kindly affected towards them that are of the same kind and nature as he is himself to contemn all sensual motions and appetites, to discern rightly all plausible fancies and imaginations, to contemplate the nature of the universe; both it, and things that are done in it.
plain: Real joy is doing what fits a person: be kind, drop cravings, test daydreams, and study the world.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If pain be an evil, either it is in regard of the body; (and that cannot be, because the body of itself is altogether insensible:) or in regard of the soul But it is in the power of the soul, to preserve her own peace and tranquillity, and not to suppose that pain is evil.
plain: If pain is bad, it is not in the body, which cannot judge. Your mind can stay calm and refuse to call pain bad.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Wipe off all idle fancies, and say unto thyself incessantly; Now if I will, it is in my power to keep out of this my soul all wickedness, all lust, and concupiscences, all trouble and confusion. But on the contrary to behold and consider all things according to their true nature, and to carry myself towards everything according to its true worth. Remember then this thy power that nature hath given thee.
plain: Clear idle thoughts and remember you can keep harm, craving, and confusion out of your mind. You can see each thing as it truly is.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Whether thou speak in the Senate or whether thou speak to any particular, let thy speech In always grave and modest. But thou must not openly and vulgarly observe that sound and exact form of speaking, concerning that which is truly good and truly civil; the vanity of the world, and of worldly men: which otherwise truth and reason doth prescribe.
plain: Whether you speak to a crowd or to one person, stay serious and modest. Do not lecture them on how empty the world is.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Augustus his court; his wife, his daughter, his nephews, his sons-in-law his sister, Agrippa, his kinsmen, his domestics, his friends; Areus, Mæcenas, his slayers of beasts for sacrifice and divination: there thou hast the death of a whole court together.
plain: Augustus, his family, his friends, and his whole court are dead together.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Alexander, Caius, Pompeius; what are these to Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates? These penetrated into the true nature of things; into all causes, and all subjects: and upon these did they exercise their power and authority. But as for those, as the extent of their error was, so far did their slavery extend.
plain: Alexander, Caius, and Pompeius were enslaved by how far they went wrong. Diogenes, Heraclitus, and Socrates saw things as they truly are.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Contract thy whole life to the measure and proportion of one single action. And if in every particular action thou dost perform what is fitting to the utmost of thy power, let it suffice thee.
plain: Shrink your whole life down to the size of one action. If you do each thing as well as you can, that is enough.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Receive temporal blessings without ostentation, when they are sent and thou shalt be able to part with them with all readiness and facility when they are taken from thee again.
plain: Take good things quietly when they come, and you can let them go easily when they are taken back.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Let not the general representation unto thyself of the wretchedness of this our mortal life, trouble thee.
plain: Do not let the wide view of how hard mortal life is bother you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What? are either Panthea or Pergamus abiding to this day by their masters' tombs? or either Chabrias or Diotimus by that of Adrianus?
plain: Panthea and Pergamus no longer wait by their masters' tombs. Chabrias and Diotimus no longer wait by the tomb of Adrianus.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou beest quick-sighted, be so in matter of judgment, and best discretion, saith he.
plain: If you are quick to notice, use that in your judgment and your best choices.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: In the whole constitution of man, I see not any virtue contrary to justice, whereby it may be resisted and opposed. But one whereby pleasure and voluptuousness may be resisted and opposed, I see: continence.
plain: Nothing in us fights fairness. Self-control is what fights pleasure and indulgence.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If thou canst but withdraw conceit and opinion concerning that which may seem hurtful and offensive, thou thyself art as safe, as safe may be. Thou thyself? and who is that? Thy reason. 'Yea, but I am not reason.' Well, be it so. However, let not thy reason or understanding admit of grief, and if there be anything in thee that is grieved, let that, (whatsoever it be,) conceive its own grief, if it can.
plain: Drop opinions about what seems harmful, and you are safe. Keep grief out of reason, and let the part that hurts carry its pain.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which is a hindrance of the senses, is an evil to the sensitive nature. That which is a hindrance of the appetitive and prosecutive faculty, is an evil to the sensitive nature.
plain: What blocks the senses harms the feeling part of you. What blocks wanting and seeking also harms that same feeling part.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What they have done, they will still do, although thou shouldst hang thyself. First; let it not trouble thee.
plain: People will keep doing the same things even if you fall apart over it. Start by not letting that trouble you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Why should I grieve myself; who never did willingly grieve any other! One thing rejoices one and another thing another.
plain: There is no need to grieve yourself if you never chose to grieve anyone. One thing cheers one person, and something else cheers another.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This time that is now present, bestow thou upon thyself. They that rather hunt for fame after death, do not consider, that those men that shall be hereafter, will be even such, as these whom now they can so hardly bear with.
plain: Give this present time to yourself. People chasing fame after death forget that future folks will be just as hard to bear as people now.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Take me and throw me where thou wilt: I am indifferent. For there also I shall have that spirit which is within me propitious; that is well pleased and fully contented both in that constant disposition, and with those particular actions, which to its own proper constitution are suitable and agreeable.
plain: Throw me wherever you want, and I stay easy. The spirit in me can still be content with its steady way and with fitting actions.

author: Marcus Aurelius
