text: Is this then a thing of that worth, that for it my soul should suffer, and become worse than it was? as either basely dejected, or disordinately affected, or confounded within itself, or terrified? What can there be, that thou shouldest so much esteem?
plain: Nothing is worth letting your mind get worse, sunk, shaken, confused, or scared. Nothing deserves that much respect from you.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Nothing can happen unto thee, which is not incidental unto thee, as thou art a man.
plain: Nothing can happen to you that does not already belong to life as a human.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Remember that thy mind is of that nature as that it becometh altogether unconquerable, when once recollected in herself, she seeks no other content than this, that she cannot be forced: yea though it so fall out, that it be even against reason itself, that it cloth bandy.
plain: Your mind becomes unbeatable when it pulls together and seeks only to stay unforced. It can keep that stand even against reason.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Keep thyself to the first bare and naked apprehensions of things, as they present themselves unto thee, and add not unto them.
plain: Stay with the first plain look at things as they show up, and do not add anything to them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Is the cucumber bitter? set it away. Brambles are in the way? avoid them. Let this suffice.
plain: If the cucumber is bitter, set it aside. If brambles block the path, go around them, and let that be enough.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not to be slack and negligent; or loose, and wanton in thy actions; nor contentious, and troublesome in thy conversation; nor to rove and wander in thy fancies and imaginations. Not basely to contract thy soul; nor boisterously to sally out with it, or furiously to launch out as it were, nor ever to want employment.
plain: Skip laziness, wild acts, rough talk, and wandering thoughts. Do not shrink your mind, burst out with it, or sit without work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: That which the nature of the universe doth busy herself about, is; that which is here, to transfer it thither, to change it, and thence again to take it away, and to carry it to another place. So that thou needest not fear any new thing. For all things are usual and ordinary; and all things are disposed by equality.
plain: The world keeps moving things, changing them, and carrying them somewhere else. Fear nothing new, since all of this is ordinary and balanced.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: 'They kill me, they cut my flesh; they persecute my person with curses.' What then?
plain: They can kill you, cut your flesh, and curse you. So what comes of that.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that knoweth not what the world is, knoweth not where he himself is. And he that knoweth not what the world was made for, cannot possibly know either what are the qualities, or what is the nature of the world.
plain: If you miss what the world is, you miss where you are. Without its purpose, you cannot know its nature either.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Not only now henceforth to have a common breath, or to hold correspondency of breath, with that air, that compasseth us about; but to have a common mind, or to hold correspondency of mind also with that rational substance, which compasseth all things.
plain: Share more than breath with the air around you. Share your mind with the reason that surrounds everything.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Wickedness in general doth not hurt the world. Particular wickedness doth not hurt any other: only unto him it is hurtful, whosoever he be that offends, unto whom in great favour and mercy it is granted, that whensoever he himself shall but first desire it, he may be presently delivered of it.
plain: Wrongdoing does not hurt the world or anyone else. It hurts only the doer, who can be free of it the moment he wants.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The sun seemeth to be shed abroad. And indeed it is diffused but not effused. For that diffusion of it is a τάσις or an extension.
plain: The sun looks poured out everywhere, but it is spread, not spilled. That spreading is a stretch, a kind of tension.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that feareth death, either feareth that he shall have no sense at all, or that his senses will not be the same. Whereas, he should rather comfort himself, that either no sense at all, and so no sense of evil; or if any sense, then another life, and so no death properly.
plain: If you fear death, you fear no feeling or a different feeling. No feeling means no harm, and a new feeling would mean another life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All men are made one for another: either then teach them better, or bear with them.
plain: People are made for one another, so either teach them better or put up with them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The motion of the mind is not as the motion of a dart. For the mind when it is wary and cautelous, and by way of diligent circumspection turneth herself many ways, may then as well be said to go straight on to the object, as when it useth no such circumspection.
plain: Your mind does not move like a thrown dart. Looking around carefully can still count as going straight toward the thing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To pierce and penetrate into the estate of every one's understanding that thou hast to do with: as also to make the estate of thine own open, and penetrable to any other.
plain: See into every mind you deal with. Keep your own mind open so any other person can see in.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Every particular nature hath content, when in its own proper course it speeds. A reasonable nature doth then speed, when first in matter of fancies and imaginations, it gives no consent to that which is either false uncertain.
plain: Each thing is content when its own path goes well. A thinking person gets there by refusing false or unclear ideas.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou hast no time nor opportunity to read. What then? Hast thou not time and opportunity to exercise thyself, not to wrong thyself; to strive against all carnal pleasures and pains, and to get the upper hand of them; to contemn honour and vainglory; and not only, not to be angry with them, whom towards thee thou doest find unsensible and unthankful; but also to have a care of them still, and of their welfare?
plain: You may have no time to read. You can still avoid hurting yourself, face pleasure and pain, drop pride, and care for ungrateful people.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Forbear henceforth to complain of the trouble of a courtly life, either in public before others, or in private by thyself.
plain: Stop complaining about the trouble of court life, both in front of others and when you are alone.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Repentance is an inward and self-reprehension for the neglect or omission of somewhat that was profitable. Now whatsoever is good, is also profitable, and it is the part of an honest virtuous man to set by it, and to make reckoning of it accordingly. But never did any honest virtuous man repent of the neglect or omission of any carnal pleasure: no carnal pleasure then is either good or profitable.
plain: Regret means you skipped something useful, and good things are useful. No honest person regrets skipping bodily pleasure, so it is not good.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that is unjust, is also impious. For the nature of the universe, having made all reasonable creatures one for another, to the end that they should do one another good; more or less according to the several persons and occasions but in nowise hurt one another: it is manifest that he that doth transgress against this her will, is guilty of impiety towards the most ancient and venerable of all the deities.
plain: Being unfair wrongs the oldest god, since the world made us to help each other and not to hurt.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Labour not as one to whom it is appointed to be wretched, nor as one that either would be pitied, or admired; but let this be thine only care and desire; so always and in all things to prosecute or to forbear, as the law of charity, or mutual society doth require.
plain: Do not work as if you are doomed, or to be pitied or admired. Only act or hold back as shared kindness asks.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: This day I did come out of all my trouble. Nay I have cast out all my trouble; it should rather be for that which troubled thee, whatsoever it was, was not without anywhere that thou shouldest come out of it, but within in thine own opinions, from whence it must be cast out, before thou canst truly and constantly be at ease.
plain: You did not leave trouble behind, because it sat inside your opinions. Cast it out from there before you can really rest.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All those things, for matter of experience are usual and ordinary; for their continuance but for a day; and for their matter, most base and filthy. As they were in the days of those whom we have buried, so are they now also, and no otherwise.
plain: These things are ordinary, brief, and dirty. They are the same now as they were for the people we have buried.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: The things themselves that affect us, they stand without doors, neither knowing anything themselves nor able to utter anything unto others concerning themselves. What then is it, that passeth verdict on them? The understanding.
plain: The things that stir you stand outside, knowing nothing and saying nothing about themselves. Your understanding is what judges them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As virtue and wickedness consist not in passion, but in action; so neither doth the true good or evil of a reasonable charitable man consist in passion, but in operation and action.
plain: Right and wrong are in the doing, not the feeling. Real good and bad for a kind person are in the doing too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To the stone that is cast up, when it comes down it is no hurt unto it; as neither benefit, when it doth ascend.
plain: A stone thrown upward is not hurt when it falls, and it gains nothing by going up.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Sift their minds and understandings, and behold what men they be, whom thou dost stand in fear of what they shall judge of thee, what they themselves judge of themselves.
plain: Look closely at the minds of people whose judgment you fear, and see what they think of themselves.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: All things that are in the world, are always in the estate of alteration. Thou also art in a perpetual change, yea and under corruption too, in some part: and so is the whole world.
plain: Everything around you keeps changing. You keep changing too, and part of you wears out, just like the world itself.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: it is not thine, but another man's sin. Why should it trouble thee? Let him look to it, whose sin it is.
plain: That mistake belongs to someone else, so it need not trouble you. Let the person who did it deal with it.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of an operation and of a purpose there is an ending, or of an action and of a purpose we say commonly, that it is at an end: from opinion also there is an absolute cessation, which is as it were the death of it.
plain: An action and its purpose can come to an end. An opinion can stop completely too, and that stop is like its death.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It were indeed more happy and comfortable, for a man to depart out of this world, having lived all his life long clear from all falsehood, dissimulation, voluptuousness, and pride.
plain: It is happier to leave this world having stayed clear of lies, pretending, indulgence, and pride.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As occasion shall require, either to thine own understanding, or to that of the universe, or to his, whom thou hast now to do with, let thy refuge be with all speed.
plain: When you need help, run fast to your own understanding, or the world's. Or run to the mind of the person you are dealing with.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: As thou thyself, whoever thou art, were made for the perfection and consummation, being a member of it, of a common society; so must every action of thine tend to the perfection and consummation of a life that is truly sociable.
plain: You were made to help complete a life shared with other people. Every action of yours should serve that shared life.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Children's anger, mere babels; wretched souls bearing up dead bodies, that they may not have their fall so soon: even as it is in that common dirge song.
plain: Their anger is childish, like puppets, or like minds holding up corpses to delay the fall. It echoes an old funeral song.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Go to the quality of the cause from which the effect doth proceed. Behold it by itself bare and naked, separated from all that is material. Then consider the utmost bounds of time that that cause, thus and thus qualified, can subsist and abide.
plain: Look at the cause behind the effect, bare and free of material things. Then ask how long a cause like that can last.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Infinite are the troubles and miseries, that thou hast already been put to, by reason of this only, because that for all happiness it did not suffice thee, or, that thou didst not account it sufficient happiness, that thy understanding did operate according to its natural constitution.
plain: You have had endless trouble only because it was not enough that your understanding worked the way it naturally does.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When any shall either impeach thee with false accusations, or hatefully reproach thee, or shall use any such carriage towards thee, get thee presently to their minds and understandings, and look in them, and behold what manner of men they be.
plain: When someone accuses you falsely or attacks you, look into their mind. See what kind of person they really are.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Up and down, from one age to another, go the ordinary things of the world; being still the same.
plain: Ordinary life rises and falls from age to age, and it stays the same.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Within a while the earth shall cover us all, and then she herself shall have her change.
plain: Soon the earth will cover all of us, and then the earth herself will change too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: And these your professed politicians, the only true practical philosophers of the world, (as they think of themselves) so full of affected gravity, or such professed lovers of virtue and honesty, what wretches be they in very deed; how vile and contemptible in themselves?
plain: These public men think they are the true practical guides, full of fake seriousness and a show of honesty. Really they are wretched and cheap.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: From some high place as it were to look down, and to behold here flocks, and there sacrifices, without number; and all kind of navigation; some in a rough and stormy sea, and some in a calm: the general differences, or different estates of things, some, that are now first upon being; the several and mutual relations of those things that are together; and some other things that are at their last.
plain: From high up you see countless flocks, sacrifices, and ships in storms or calm. You also see things starting, things tied together, and things ending.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Thou must not in matter of death carry thyself scornfully, but as one that is well pleased with it, as being one of those things that nature hath appointed.
plain: Do not meet death with scorn. Meet it gladly, as one of the things nature has set in place.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Many of those things that trouble and straiten thee, it is in thy power to cut off, as wholly depending from mere conceit and opinion; and then thou shalt have room enough.
plain: Many things that squeeze you come only from opinion, and you can cut them off. Then you will have room enough.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To comprehend the whole world together in thy mind, and the whole course of this present age to represent it unto thyself, and to fix thy thoughts upon the sudden change of every particular object.
plain: Hold the whole world and this age in your mind. Fix your thoughts on the sudden change of each thing.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: What are their minds and understandings; and what the things that they apply themselves unto: what do they love, and what do they hate for? Fancy to thyself the estate of their souls openly to be seen. When they think they hurt them shrewdly, whom they speak ill of; and when they think they do them a very good turn, whom they commend and extol: O how full are they then of conceit, and opinion!
plain: See what they love and hate, and picture their minds wide open. They swell up when they think insults wound or praise helps.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Loss and corruption, is in very deed nothing else but change and alteration; and that is it, which the nature of the universe doth most delight in, by which, and according to which, whatsoever is done, is well done.
plain: Loss and decay are really only change, and the world loves that change. By that change, whatever happens is done well.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: How base and putrid, every common matter is! Water, dust, and from the mixture of these bones, and all that loathsome stuff that our bodies do consist of: so subject to be infected, and corrupted.
plain: Everyday matter is low and rotten: water, dust, bones, and the gross mix bodies are made of. It spoils so easily.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Will this querulousness, this murmuring, this complaining and dissembling never be at an end?
plain: This whining, muttering, complaining, and pretending never seems to end.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is all one to see these things for a hundred of years together or but for three years.
plain: Seeing this for a hundred years matches seeing it for just three.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Sayest thou unto that rational part, Thou art dead; corruption hath taken hold on thee? Doth it then also void excrements? Doth it like either oxen, or sheep, graze or feed; that it also should be mortal, as well as the body?
plain: Do not call your thinking part dead and rotten. It neither grazes nor passes waste, so it is not mortal like the body.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: He that sinneth, sinneth unto himself. He that is unjust, hurts himself, in that he makes himself worse than he was before. Not he only that committeth, but he also that omitteth something, is oftentimes unjust.
plain: The person who does wrong hurts himself by becoming worse. Leaving something undone can make you unfair too.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either the Gods can do nothing for us at all, or they can still and allay all the distractions and distempers of thy mind.
plain: Either the gods offer us no help, or they can settle every restless feeling in your mind.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: It is common to all trades and professions to mind and intend that only, which now they are about, and the instrument whereby they work.
plain: Every trade pays attention only to the job at hand and to the tool used for that work.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: When at any time thou art offended with any one's impudency, put presently this question to thyself: 'What?
plain: When someone's shamelessness offends you, stop and ask yourself what this is.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: If my present apprehension of the object be right, and my present action charitable, and this, towards whatsoever doth proceed from God, be my present disposition, to be well pleased with it, it sufficeth.
plain: If you see the thing rightly, act with kindness, and feel glad about whatever comes from God, that is enough.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: To wipe away fancy, to use deliberation, to quench concupiscence, to keep the mind free to herself.
plain: Clear away daydreams, think things through, cool your cravings, and keep your mind free.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Of all unreasonable creatures, there is but one unreasonable soul; and of all that are reasonable, but one reasonable soul, divided betwixt them all.
plain: All unthinking creatures share one unthinking mind, and all thinking ones share one thinking mind, split among them.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Man, God, the world, every one in their kind, bear some fruits. All things have their proper time to bear.
plain: People, God, and the world each bear fruit in their own way. Everything has its own time to bear fruit.

author: Marcus Aurelius
text: Either teach them better if it be in thy power; or if it be not, remember that for this use, to bear with them patiently, was mildness and goodness granted unto thee.
plain: Teach them better if you can. If you cannot, remember that patience with them is the mildness and goodness given to you.

author: Seneca
text: All men, brother Gallio, wish to live happily, but are dull at perceiving exactly what it is that makes life happy: and so far is it from being easy to attain the happiness that the more eagerly a man struggles to reach it the further he departs from it, if he takes the wrong road; for, since this leads in the opposite direction, his very swiftness carries him all the further away.
plain: Everyone wants a happy life, but few see what actually makes it happy. Rushing down the wrong road only carries you farther away.

author: Seneca
text: All these are dissipated by virtue, which plucks a man by the ear, and measures the value of pleasures before she permits them to be used; nor does she set much store by those which she allows to pass current, for she merely allows their use, and her cheerfulness is not due to her use of them, but to her moderation in using them.
plain: Good sense pulls you by the ear and weighs pleasure first. The cheer comes from holding back, not from using it a lot.

author: Seneca
text: When I say that I do nothing for the sake of pleasure, I allude to that wise man, whom alone you admit to be capable of pleasure: now I do not call a man wise who is overcome by anything, let alone by pleasure: yet, if engrossed by pleasure, how will he resist toil, danger, want, and all the ills which surround and threaten the life of man?
plain: A wise person does nothing for pleasure and is not beaten by it. If pleasure owns him, he cannot face hard work, danger, or lack.

author: Seneca
text: The pleasures of wise men, on the other hand, are mild, decorous, verging on dullness, kept under restraint and scarcely noticeable, and are neither invited to come nor received with honour when they come of their own accord, nor are they welcomed with any delight by those whom they visit, who mix them up with their lives and fill up empty spaces with them, like an amusing farce in the intervals of serious business.
plain: Wise pleasures stay mild, quiet, and almost dull. They are not invited or cheered, and they only fill gaps between serious work.

author: Seneca
text: I myself believe, though my Stoic comrades would be unwilling to hear me say so, that the teaching of Epicurus was upright and holy, and even, if you examine it narrowly, stern: for this much talked of pleasure is reduced to a very narrow compass, and he bids pleasure submit to the same law which we bid virtue do⁠—I mean, to obey nature.
plain: Friends may hate this, but I find Epicurus upright, holy, and strict. Pleasure stays small and must obey nature, as good conduct does.

author: Seneca
text: Let virtue lead the way and bear the standard: we shall have pleasure for all that, but we shall be her masters and controllers; she may win some concessions from us, but will not force us to do anything.
plain: Let good choices go first and carry the flag. You can still enjoy life, but you stay in charge of that joy.

author: Seneca
text: Even the joy which arises from virtue, although it be a good thing, yet is not a part of absolute good, any more than cheerfulness or peace of mind, which are indeed good things, but which merely follow the highest good, and do not contribute to its perfection, although they are generated by the noblest causes.
plain: Joy from doing right is good, but it is not the highest good. A calm mind only follows that good and does not complete it.

author: Seneca
text: True happiness, therefore, consists in virtue: and what will this virtue bid you do?
plain: Real happiness sits in good choices. What those choices ask of you still matters.

author: Seneca
text: Why do you pay regard to common rumour, and feel annoyed by calumnious gossip? why is your estate more elaborately kept than its natural use requires? why do you not dine according to your own maxims? why is your furniture smarter than it need be? why do you drink wine that is older than yourself? why are your grounds laid out?
plain: You care about gossip and keep a fancier home than you need. Your meals and wine are for show, not your own rules.

author: Seneca
text: You argue about the life and death of another, and yelp at the name of men whom some peculiarly noble quality has rendered great, just as tiny curs do at the approach of strangers: for it is to your interest that no one should appear to be good, as if virtue in another were a reproach to all your crimes.
plain: You bark at great people like a small dog at strangers. Their good choices make your own mess look worse.

author: Seneca
text: Let us therefore inquire, not what is most commonly done, but what is best for us to do, and what will establish us in the possession of undying happiness, not what is approved of by the vulgar, the worst possible exponents of truth.
plain: Look for what is best for you, not what most people do. Lasting happiness does not come from the crowd's approval.

author: Seneca
text: Men deserve praise for engaging in profitable studies, even though they stop short of producing any results.
plain: You deserve credit for useful study, even when you stop before any results show up.

author: Seneca
text: Why does he say that wealth ought to be despised and yet possess it? that life should be despised, and yet live? that health should be despised, and yet guard it with the utmost care, and wish it to be as good as possible?
plain: He says money, life, and health should be looked down on, yet he keeps them and guards health carefully.

author: Seneca
text: Who can doubt, however, that the wise man, if he is rich, has a wider field for the development of his powers than if he is poor, seeing that in the latter case the only virtue which he can display is that of neither being perverted nor crushed by his poverty, whereas if he has riches, he will have a wide field for the exhibition of temperance, generosity, laboriousness, methodical arrangement, and grandeur.
plain: If you are wise and poor, you mainly show that lack neither twists nor crushes you. Money gives room for generosity, hard work, and order.

author: Seneca
text: Cease, then, forbidding philosophers to possess money: no one has condemned wisdom to poverty.
plain: Stop telling wise people they cannot have money. Nobody sentenced wisdom to being poor.

author: Seneca
text: He who believes giving to be an easy matter, is mistaken: it offers very great difficulties, if we bestow our bounty rationally, and do not scatter it impulsively and at random.
plain: If you think giving is easy, you are wrong. Careful giving is hard, and random gifts skip that work.

author: Seneca
text: Learn, then, since we both agree that they are desirable, what my reason is amongst counting them among good things, and in what respects I should behave differently to you if I possessed them.
plain: We both agree these things are worth wanting. Hear why I still call them good, and how I would act if I had them.

author: Seneca
text: You accustom yourself to them and cling to them as if somebody had promised that they should be yours forever, but a wise man never thinks so much about poverty as when he is surrounded by riches.
plain: You cling to nice things as if they were yours forever. A wise person thinks hardest about lack when money is all around.

author: Seneca
text: Praise good men, if you are able: if not, pass them by in silence: if indeed you take pleasure in this offensive abusiveness, fall foul of one another: for when you rave against Heaven, I do not say that you commit sacrilege, but you waste your time.
plain: Praise good people if you can, or stay quiet. If you enjoy nasty talk, fight each other, because raging at heaven only wastes your time.

author: Seneca
text: Let us seek for some blessing, which does not merely look fine, but is sound and good throughout alike, and most beautiful in the parts which are least seen: let us unearth this.
plain: Look for a good thing that is solid all the way through, not just pretty on the outside. The hidden parts should be the finest.

author: Seneca
text: Our highest good may also be defined otherwise; that is to say, the same idea may be expressed in different language.
plain: You can put the highest good into other words. The idea stays the same when the wording changes.

author: Seneca
text: With them you may class men whose dull nature and want of self-knowledge reduces them to the level of cattle, mere animals: there is no difference between the one and the other, because the latter have no reason, while the former have only a corrupted form of it, crooked and cunning to their own hurt.
plain: Some people are like animals because they barely know themselves. Animals have no reason, and these people use a twisted kind that hurts them.

author: Seneca
text: The happy man, therefore, is he who can make a right judgment in all things: he is happy who in his present circumstances, whatever they may be, is satisfied and on friendly terms with the conditions of his life.
plain: A happy person judges things well. You are happy when you are at peace with your life as it is right now.

author: Seneca
text: Even those very people who declare the highest good to be in the belly, see what a dishonourable position they have assigned to it: and therefore they say that pleasure cannot be parted from virtue, and that no one can either live honourably without living cheerfully, nor yet live cheerfully without living honourably.
plain: People who put the highest good in the belly know that place is low. They say joy and living well cannot be split apart.

author: Seneca
text: What answer are we to make to the reflection that pleasure belongs to good and bad men alike, and that bad men take as much delight in their shame as good men in noble things?
plain: Pleasure belongs to good people and bad people alike. Bad people enjoy their shame as much as good people enjoy fine things.

author: Seneca
text: For this cause reason will never call to its aid blind and fierce impulses, over whom she herself possesses no authority, and which she never can restrain save by setting against them similar and equally powerful passions, as for example, fear against anger, anger against sloth, greed against timidity.
plain: Clear thinking will not call on blind, fierce urges it cannot control. It would only fight them with other strong feelings, like fear against anger.

author: Seneca
text: What, indeed, is it except anger, so ruinous to itself, that overthrows barbarians, who have so much more bodily strength than we, and are so much better able to endure fatigue?
plain: Anger wrecks itself, yet it has toppled peoples stronger than us. They had tougher bodies and could last longer.

author: Seneca
text: Why do you fear that filial piety will not prove a sufficient spur to him even without anger?
plain: Family love can push a person well enough, even without anger.

author: Seneca
text: Moreover, qualities which we ought to possess become better and more desirable the more extensive they are: if justice is a good thing, no one will say that it would be better if any part were subtracted from it; if bravery is a good thing, no one would wish it to be in any way curtailed: consequently the greater anger is, the better it is, for whoever objected to a good thing being increased?
plain: Good traits get better the more of them you have. If anger were good like fairness or courage, more of it would be better too.

author: Seneca
text: It is impossible, says Theophrastus, for a good man not to be angry with bad men.
plain: Theophrastus says a good person cannot help being angry at bad people.

author: Seneca
text: The sinner ought, therefore, to be corrected both by warning and by force, both by gentle and harsh means, and may be made a better man both towards himself and others by chastisement, but not by anger: for who is angry with the patient whose wounds he is tending?
plain: Correct someone by warning or by force, gently or harshly. A healer is not angry at the patient, and anger does not make people better.

author: Seneca
text: We do not, therefore, need an angry chastiser to punish the erring and wicked: for since anger is a crime of the mind, it is not right that sins should be punished by sin.
plain: You need no angry punisher for people who mess up. Anger is a wrong in the mind, so it should not punish wrong.

author: Seneca
text: These arms, which Aristotle assigns to virtue, fight of their own accord, do not wait to be seized by the hand, and possess a man instead of being possessed by him.
plain: The weapons Aristotle gives to right action fight on their own. They take hold of you instead of waiting for your hand.

author: Seneca
text: Irascibility, I say, has this fault⁠—it is loath to be ruled: it is angry with the truth itself, if it comes to light against its will: it assails those whom it has marked for its victims with shouting and riotous noise and gesticulation of the entire body, together with reproaches and curses.
plain: A hot temper hates being ruled, and it gets mad at the truth. It shouts, waves, and curses at people it targets.

author: Seneca
text: Neither ought it to be believed that anger contributes anything to magnanimity: what it gives is not magnanimity but vain glory.
plain: Do not believe anger adds anything to real greatness. What it gives is empty showing off.

author: Seneca
text: There is therefore nothing great or noble in anger, even when it seems to be powerful and to contemn both gods and men alike.
plain: Anger holds nothing great or noble. That stays true even when it looks strong and sneers at gods and people.

author: Seneca
text: In the next place, no one is so low in station as not to be able to hope to inflict punishment even upon the greatest of men: we all are powerful for mischief.
plain: Nobody is so low that they cannot hope to hurt even the greatest people. All of us can do harm.

author: Seneca
text: What anger is has been sufficiently explained. The difference between it and irascibility is evident: it is the same as that between a drunken man and a drunkard; between a frightened man and a coward.
plain: Anger and a hot temper differ like being drunk once and living drunk. One scare is not the same as being a coward.

author: Seneca
text: We have now finished our enquiry as to what anger is, whether it exists in any other creature besides man, what the difference is between it and irascibility, and how many forms it possesses. Let us now enquire whether anger be in accordance with nature, and whether it be useful and worth entertaining in some measure.
plain: What anger is, and how it differs from a hot temper, is settled. Now ask whether anger is natural and worth keeping.

author: Seneca
text: We char crooked spearshafts to straighten them, and force them by driving in wedges, not in order to break them, but to take the bends out of them; and, in like manner, by applying pain to the body or mind we correct dispositions which have been rendered crooked by vice.
plain: We heat bent spears to straighten them, not to snap them. Pain on the body or the mind can unbend a crooked character too.

author: Seneca
text: May it not be that, although anger be not natural, it may be right to adopt it, because it often proves useful?
plain: Even if anger is not natural, it might still be right to use because it often helps.

author: Seneca
text: My first book, Novatus, had a more abundant subject: for carriages roll easily down hill: now we must proceed to drier matters.
plain: The first book had an easier subject, like a cart rolling downhill. Now we have to take on drier stuff.

author: Seneca
text: You will rather think that we should not be angry with people’s faults; for what shall we say of one who is angry with those who stumble in the dark, or with deaf people who cannot hear his orders, or with children, because they forget their duty and interest themselves in the games and silly jokes of their companions?
plain: Do not get angry at people's slips. That is like raging at a stumble in the dark, a deaf person, or a child at play.

author: Seneca
text: If, again, it is without strength, it is much more exposed to contempt, and cannot avoid ridicule: for what is more flat than anger when it breaks out into meaningless ravings?
plain: If anger has no strength, people look down on it and laugh. Nothing falls flatter than anger that spills into empty raving.

author: Seneca
text: He may be protected against the inclement time of the year by dwelling in a favoured spot, or he may have so trained his body to endurance that it feels neither heat nor cold.
plain: You might dodge rough weather by living in a sheltered spot. Or you might train until heat and cold barely touch you.

author: Seneca
text: There is no reason why we should seek to defend such a passion as this or excuse its excesses by declaring it to be either useful or unavoidable.
plain: There is no good reason to defend this feeling or excuse its excess by calling it useful or unavoidable.

author: Seneca
text: Anger, then, must never become a habit with us, but we may sometimes affect to be angry when we wish to rouse up the dull minds of those whom we address, just as we rouse up horses who are slow at starting with goads and firebrands.
plain: Anger should never become your habit. You may sometimes act angry to wake a dull mind, the way a slow horse is stirred to start.

author: Seneca
text: In like manner, dispositions which are naturally bold produce irritability, and, being hot and fiery, have no mean or trivial qualities, but their energy is misdirected, as happens with all those who without training come to the front by their natural advantages alone, whose minds, unless they be brought under control, degenerate from a courageous temper into habits of rashness and reckless daring.
plain: Bold natures get irritable, hot, and strong, but their energy goes the wrong way. Without training, courage slides into rash daring.

author: Seneca
text: Those animals, urges our opponent, are held to be the most generous who have large capacity for anger.
plain: The other side says the noblest animals are the ones most capable of anger.

author: Seneca
text: A man ought to be neither robber nor victim, neither tenderhearted nor cruel. The former belongs to an over-weak mind, the latter to an over-hard one.
plain: Skip being a robber or a victim, and skip being too soft or cruel. Softness is a weak mind, and cruelty is a hard one.

author: Seneca
text: Now that we have discussed the questions propounded concerning anger, let us pass on to the consideration of its remedies.
plain: Now that the questions about anger are discussed, we can move on to its remedies.

author: Seneca
text: A hot mind is naturally the most prone to anger: for as there are four elements, consisting of fire, air, earth, and water, so there are powers corresponding and equivalent to each of these, namely, hot, cold, dry, and moist.
plain: A hot mind, like fire, is the most likely to get angry. Cold, dry, and moist match air, earth, and water.

author: Seneca
text: Whither, say you, does this inquiry tend? That we may know what anger is: for if it springs up against our will, it never will yield to reason: because all the motions which take place without our volition are beyond our control and unavoidable, such as shivering when cold water is poured over us, or shrinking when we are touched in certain places.
plain: This question asks what anger is. If it rises against your will, reason cannot stop it, like a shiver when cold water hits you.

author: Seneca
text: But just as nature makes some men prone to anger, so there are many other causes which have the same power as nature.
plain: Nature makes some people quick to anger, and many other causes can do the same thing.

author: Seneca
text: It is, I assure you, of the greatest service to boys that they should be soundly brought up, yet to regulate their education is difficult, because it is our duty to be careful neither to cherish a habit of anger in them, nor to blunt the edge of their spirit.
plain: Raising boys well matters a lot, but guiding that training is hard. You must not feed their anger or dull their drive.

author: Seneca
text: These precepts, however, apply to our children: in ourselves the accident of birth and our education no longer admits of either mistakes or advice; we must deal with what follows.
plain: Those lessons fit children. For you, birth and schooling are already done, so you deal with what comes next.

author: Seneca
text: Everyone knows the story of the tyrannicide who, being caught before he had accomplished his task, and being tortured by Hippias to make him betray his accomplices, named the friends of the tyrant who stood around, and everyone to whom he knew the tyrant’s safety was especially dear.
plain: Everyone knows the man caught before he could kill the ruler. Under torture he named the ruler's own friends as helpers.

author: Seneca
text: Readiness to believe what we hear causes very great mischief; we ought often not even to listen, because in some cases it is better to be deceived than to suspect deceit.
plain: Believing everything you hear causes real harm. Sometimes it is better not to listen, because being fooled can beat suspecting a trick.

author: Seneca
text: Another consequence of this will be, that we shall not be exasperated by the slightest and most contemptible trifles.
plain: Another result is that tiny, silly things will not set you off.

author: Seneca
text: We are angry, either with those who can, or with those who cannot do us an injury.
plain: You get angry either at people who can hurt you, or at people who cannot.

author: Seneca
text: There are some things which are unable to hurt us, and whose power is exclusively beneficial and salutary, as, for example, the immortal gods, who neither wish nor are able to do harm: for their temperament is naturally gentle and tranquil, and no more likely to wrong others than to wrong themselves.
plain: Some powers cannot hurt you and only help, like the gods. They are gentle, and they will not harm others or themselves.

author: Seneca
text: If we desire to be impartial judges of all that takes place, we must first convince ourselves of this, that no one of us is faultless: for it is from this that most of our indignation proceeds.
plain: To judge fairly, first admit that none of us is without fault. Most of your anger starts from forgetting that.

author: Seneca
text: The greatest remedy for anger is delay: beg anger to grant you this at the first, not in order that it may pardon the offence, but that it may form a right judgment about it:⁠—if it delays, it will come to an end.
plain: The best fix for anger is waiting. Ask for that pause so you can judge the hurt fairly, and the anger fades.

author: Seneca
text: None of these things which casually influence the mind deserve to be called passions: the mind, if I may so express it, rather suffers passions to act upon itself than forms them.
plain: A passing stir in the mind is not a real passion. The mind lets a passion act on it more than it forms one.

author: Seneca
text: Some offences we ourselves witness: in these cases let us examine the disposition and purpose of the offender.
plain: When you see the offence yourself, look at the person's mood and what they meant to do.

author: Seneca
text: There are, as I have stated, two cases which produce anger: first, when we appear to have received an injury, about which enough has been said, and, secondly, when we appear to have been treated unjustly: this must now be discussed.
plain: Two things stir anger. We already covered feeling hurt, and now we take up feeling that you were treated unfairly.

author: Seneca
text: In the latter case it is a shame to be conquered; in the former it is a shame to conquer.
plain: In the later case, losing is a shame. In the earlier case, winning is a shame.

author: Seneca
text: The wrongs of the powerful must not only be borne, but borne with a cheerful countenance: they will repeat the wrong if they think they have inflicted it.
plain: Bear wrongs from powerful people, and look cheerful about it. They will repeat the hurt if they think they got to you.

author: Seneca
text: We must, therefore, refrain from anger, whether he who provokes us be on a level with ourselves, or above us, or below us.
plain: Hold back from anger whether the person who sets you off is equal to you, above you, or below you.

author: Seneca
text: Does anyone wish to strike his enemy so hard, as to leave his own hand in the wound, and not to be able to recover his balance after the blow? yet such a weapon is anger: it is scarcely possible to draw it back.
plain: Anger is a blow that leaves your hand stuck in the wound. You can barely pull it back or find your balance.

author: Seneca
text: Furthermore, that you may know in what manner passions begin and swell and gain spirit, learn that the first emotion is involuntary, and is, as it were, a preparation for a passion, and a threatening of one.
plain: Passions grow and gather force. The first feeling is not chosen, and it only warns that a stronger one may follow.

author: Seneca
text: We must also enquire whether those whose cruelty knows no bounds, and who delight in shedding human blood, are angry when they kill people from whom they have received no injury, and who they themselves do not think have done them any injury; such as were Apollodorus or Phalaris.
plain: Ask if people who love bloodshed feel rage while killing folks who never hurt them. Apollodorus and Phalaris were like that.

author: Seneca
text: To rejoice and be glad is the proper and natural function of virtue: it is as much beneath her dignity to be angry, as to mourn: now, sorrow is the companion of anger, and all anger ends in sorrow, either from remorse or from failure.
plain: Being glad comes naturally to a good person, and anger is as low as grief. Sadness follows anger, from regret or from failure.

author: Seneca
text: What, too, can be more unworthy of the wise man, than that his passions should depend upon the wickedness of others?
plain: Nothing is less fitting for a wise person than letting their feelings hang on other people's bad behavior.

author: Seneca
text: Why need I dwell upon individual cases? Be assured, when you see the forum crowded with a multitude, the Saepta swarming with people, or the great Circus, in which the greater part of the people find room to show themselves at once, that among them there are as many vices as there are men.
plain: In a packed crowd, at the market or the circus, there are as many bad habits as there are people.

author: Seneca
text: The wise man will never cease to be angry, if he once begins, so full is every place of vices and crimes.
plain: If a wise person starts getting angry, they will never stop, because every place is full of wrongs and crimes.

author: Seneca
text: We will now, my Novatus, attempt to do that which you so especially long to do, that is, to drive out anger from our minds, or at all events to curb it and restrain its impulses.
plain: Now we do what you most want. We push anger out of our minds, or at least hold it back.

author: Seneca
text: That which is diseased can never bear to be handled without complaining: it is best, therefore, to apply remedies to oneself as soon as we feel that anything is wrong, to allow oneself as little licence as possible in speech, and to restrain one’s impetuosity: now it is easy to detect the first growth of our passions: the symptoms precede the disorder.
plain: A sore spot complains when touched, so treat yourself when something first feels wrong. Signs come early, so say little and hold your temper back.

author: Seneca
text: It is better not to see or to hear everything: many causes of offence may pass by us, most of which are disregarded by the man who ignores them.
plain: Skip some of what you could see or hear. Plenty of slights pass by the person who pays them no mind.

author: Seneca
text: A large part of mankind manufacture their own grievances either by entertaining unfounded suspicions or by exaggerating trifles.
plain: Lots of people build their own hurts. They suspect things with no basis, or they blow tiny stuff way up.

author: Seneca
text: Fight hard with yourself, and if you cannot conquer anger, do not let it conquer you: you have begun to get the better of it if it does not show itself, if it is not given vent.
plain: Fight hard with yourself. If you cannot beat anger, keep it from beating you, and you are ahead when it stays hidden.

author: Seneca
text: King Cambyses was excessively addicted to wine. Præxaspes was the only one of his closest friends who advised him to drink more sparingly, pointing out how shameful a thing drunkenness was in a king, upon whom all eyes and ears were fixed.
plain: King Cambyses drank far too much. Only Praexaspes, a close friend, told him to drink less, since a watched king looks shameful when drunk.

author: Seneca
text: I have no doubt that Harpagus must have given some such advice to the king of the Persians and of himself, in anger at which the king placed Harpagus’s own children before him on the dinner-table for him to eat, and asked him from time to time, whether he liked the seasoning.
plain: Harpagus likely gave the Persian king the same advice. Angry, the king made him eat his children and kept asking if the seasoning pleased him.

author: Seneca
text: Would to heaven that such savagery had contented itself with foreign examples, and that barbarity in anger and punishment had not been imported with other outlandish vices into our Roman manners!
plain: I wish that kind of savagery had stayed with foreign examples. Cruel anger and punishment should not have entered Roman ways.

author: Seneca
text: It is to the purpose that we should know how haughtily his cruelty was exercised, although someone might suppose that we are wandering from the subject and embarking on a digression; but this digression is itself connected with unusual outbursts of anger.
plain: It helps to see the proud way he practiced cruelty. This side story still connects to rare bursts of anger.

author: Seneca
text: Thus, the king of the Persians cut off the noses of a whole nation in Syria, wherefore the place is called Rhinocolura.
plain: The Persian king removed every nose from a whole people in Syria. That spot got the name Rhinocolura because of it.

author: Seneca
text: This man was angry with an unknown and inoffensive nation, which nevertheless was able to feel his wrath; but Cyrus was angry with a river.
plain: This man was angry at a harmless people he did not know, and they could feel it. Cyrus got angry at a river.

author: Seneca
text: These should be regarded as examples to be avoided, and what I am about to relate, on the contrary, to be followed, being examples of gentle and lenient conduct in men who both had reasons for anger and power to avenge themselves.
plain: Treat those stories as examples to avoid. Copy the gentle people next, who had cause to be angry and power to hit back.

author: Seneca
text: Have I more authority in my own house than the Emperor Augustus possessed throughout the world? yet he was satisfied with leaving the society of his maligner.
plain: Augustus ruled the world and only walked away from his critic. You do not have more power at home than that.

author: Seneca
text: As it is a consolation to a humble man in trouble that the greatest are subject to reverses of fortune, and a man weeps more calmly over his dead son in the corner of his hovel if he sees a piteous funeral proceed out of the palace as well; so one bears injury or insult more calmly if one remembers that no power is so great as to be above the reach of harm.
plain: A poor man weeps more calmly for his son if a palace mourns too. You bear insult more calmly, since no power is above harm.

author: Seneca
text: Besides, what you intend to do is to endure both injury and anger. Why do you bear with the delirium of a sick man, or the ravings of a madman, or the impudent blows of a child?
plain: You plan to endure both the hurt and the anger. You already bear a sick person's raving, a mad fit, or a child's rude blow.

author: Seneca
text: How far better is it to heal an injury than to avenge it? Revenge takes up much time, and throws itself in the way of many injuries while it is smarting under one.
plain: Healing a hurt is far better than paying it back. Revenge eats time and walks you into more hurts while one still stings.

author: Seneca
text: It is shameful to hate him whom you praise: but how much more shameful is it to hate a man for something for which he deserves to be pitied?
plain: Hating someone you also praise is a shame. Hating them for a thing that deserves pity is even worse.

author: Seneca
text: It is therefore essential to prove its unseemliness and ferocity, and to place distinctly before our eyes how monstrous a thing it is that one man should rage against another, with what frantic violence he rushes to destroy alike himself and his foe, and overthrows those very things whose fall he himself must share.
plain: See how ugly and fierce anger is. Raging at someone wrecks you, them, and the things that fall on you too.

author: Seneca
text: How much better is it to observe how trifling, how inoffensive are the first beginnings of anger?
plain: It is much better to notice how small and harmless anger is at the very start.

author: Seneca
text: No man is satisfied with his own lot if he fixes his attention on that of another: and this leads to our being angry even with the gods, because somebody precedes us, though we forget of how many we take precedence, and that when a man envies few people, he must be followed in the background by a huge crowd of people who envy him.
plain: Staring at someone else's lot leaves you unhappy. You may get angry at the gods and forget the crowd behind you.

author: Seneca
text: Let different qualities in different people keep us from quarrelling with them: let us fear to be angry with some, feel ashamed of being angry with others, and disdain to be angry with others.
plain: Let each person's traits keep you from a fight. Fear being angry with some, feel shame with others, and refuse it with the rest.

author: Seneca
text: Come now, let us enumerate the other causes of anger: they are food, drink, and the showy apparatus connected with them, words, insults, disrespectful movements of the body, suspicions, obstinate cattle, lazy slaves, and spiteful construction put upon other men’s words, so that even the gift of language to mankind becomes reckoned among the wrongs of nature.
plain: Food, drink, fancy display, insults, rude moves, suspicion, stubborn animals, and lazy workers all stir anger. Twisting someone's words counts as a wrong too.

author: Seneca
text: You are indignant at being answered back by your slave, your freedman, your wife, or your client: and then you complain of the State having lost the freedom which you have destroyed in your own house: then again if he is silent when you question him, you call it sullen obstinacy.
plain: You get mad when people at home answer back, then mourn public freedom you killed there. If they stay silent, you call it sulking.

author: Seneca
text: All our senses should be educated into strength: they are naturally able to endure much, provided that the spirit forbears to spoil them.
plain: Train your senses to be strong. They can already handle a lot, as long as your mind does not spoil them.

author: Seneca
text: At the dinner-table some jokes and sayings intended to give you pain have been directed against you: avoid feasting with low people.
plain: If jokes at dinner are meant to hurt you, stay away from meals with rough company.

author: Seneca
text: Someone has offered you an insult? Not a greater one, probably, than was offered to the Stoic philosopher Diogenes, in whose face an insolent young man spat just when he was lecturing upon anger.
plain: Your insult is probably no worse than a rude young man spitting in Diogenes's face. He was talking about anger then.

author: Seneca
text: We have now succeeded, my Novatus, in properly regulating our own minds: they either do not feel anger or are above it: let us next see how we may soothe the wrath of others, for we do not only wish to be whole, but to heal.
plain: Our minds are set, free of anger or above it. Next we calm others too, since we want to heal, not only be well.

author: Seneca
text: There may be some doubt about the others, but at any rate no passion has a worse look.
plain: You might doubt the other feelings, but no feeling has a worse look.

author: Seneca
text: I myself, by Hercules, am scandalized at your treatment and am grieved beyond measure, but we must wait for a proper opportunity.
plain: I am shocked and deeply sad about how you were treated, but we have to wait for the right moment.

author: Seneca
text: Let us be free from this evil, let us clear our minds of it, and extirpate root and branch a passion which grows again wherever the smallest particle of it finds a resting-place.
plain: Let us get free of this bad feeling. Clear it from your mind, because even a tiny bit left behind grows back.

author: Seneca
text: Instead of acting thus, why do you not rather draw together what there is of your short life, and keep it peaceful for others and for yourself? why do you not rather make yourself beloved by everyone while you live, and regretted by everyone when you die?
plain: Why not gather your remaining years and keep them calm for you and others? Be loved while you live, and missed when you go.

author: Seneca
text: You ask me, whither does all this tend? To prove, I answer, that no one should imagine himself to be safe from anger, seeing that it rouses up even those who are naturally gentle and quiet to commit savage and violent acts.
plain: You ask where this is heading. It shows nobody is safe from anger, since it can push even gentle quiet people into harsh acts.

author: Seneca
text: There is no greater proof of magnanimity than that nothing which befalls you should be able to move you to anger.
plain: Nothing shows a big heart more clearly than this. Nothing that happens to you can push you into anger.

author: Seneca
text: Be assured that the same rule applies both to public and private life: simple and manageable undertakings proceed according to the pleasure of the person in charge of them, but enormous ones, beyond his capacity to manage, are not easily undertaken.
plain: One rule fits public life and private life. Easy jobs go as the leader wishes, but huge ones they cannot handle do not start easily.

author: Seneca
text: Since we know not how to endure an injury, let us take care not to receive one: we should live with the quietest and easiest-tempered persons, not with anxious or with sullen ones: for our own habits are copied from those with whom we associate, and just as some bodily diseases are communicated by touch, so also the mind transfers its vices to its neighbours.
plain: Since you cannot bear a hurt, avoid getting one. Live with calm people, not worried or sour ones, because habits and moods spread.

author: Seneca
text: Irascible men ought not to meddle with the more serious class of occupations, or, at any rate, ought to stop short of weariness in the pursuit of them; their mind ought not to be engaged upon hard subjects, but handed over to pleasing arts: let it be softened by reading poetry, and interested by legendary history: let it be treated with luxury and refinement.
plain: Hot-tempered people should skip heavy work, or stop before they wear out. Soften the mind with poems, old stories, and some comfort.

author: Seneca
text: … why do they with great unanimity recommend vices to us? even though we attempt nothing else that would do us good, yet retirement in itself will be beneficial to us: we shall be better men when taken singly⁠—and if so, what an advantage it will be to retire into the society of the best of men, and to choose some example by which we may guide our lives!
plain: Why do people all push bad habits? Time apart still helps you, and time with the best gives you someone to copy.

author: Seneca
text: Now I will prove to you that I am not deserting the tenets of the Stoics: for they themselves have not deserted them: and yet I should be able to plead a very good excuse even if I did follow, not their precepts, but their examples.
plain: I am not dropping their teaching, because they never dropped it. Even copying their actions instead of their words would be a fair excuse.

author: Seneca
text: I will show that this is approved of by the Stoics also, not that I have laid any commandment upon myself to do nothing contrary to the teaching of Zeno and Chrysippus, but because the matter itself allows me to follow the precepts of those men; for if one always follows the precepts of one man, one ceases to be a debater and becomes a partisan.
plain: This fits their teaching because the subject allows it, not because I vowed to follow Zeno or Chrysippus. Copying one man makes you a fan.

author: Seneca
text: This may be that of the Athenians or Carthaginians, or of any other city which does not belong to all men but to some especial ones.
plain: This may be Athens or Carthage, or any other city that belongs to some people and not to everyone.

author: Seneca
text: We have a habit of saying that the highest good is to live according to nature: now nature has produced us for both purposes, for contemplation and for action.
plain: People often say the best life follows nature. Nature made us both to think and to act.

author: Seneca
text: It is by no means desirable that one should merely strive to accumulate property without any love of virtue, or do nothing but hard work without any cultivation of the intellect, for these things ought to be combined and blended together; and, similarly, virtue placed in leisure without action is but an incomplete and feeble good thing, because she never displays what she has learned.
plain: Hoarding money without caring what is right, or only grinding without learning, misses the point. Sitting idle never shows what you learned.

author: Seneca
text: Moreover, there are three kinds of life, and it is a stock question which of the three is the best: the first is devoted to pleasure, the second to contemplation, the third to action.
plain: Life comes in three kinds, and people keep asking which wins: pleasure, thinking, or doing.

author: Seneca
text: Add to this that, according to the doctrine of Chrysippus, a man may live at leisure: I do not say that he ought to endure leisure, but that he ought to choose it.
plain: Chrysippus says you may live at rest. You should choose that rest, not merely put up with it.

author: Seneca
text: These remarks of mine apply only to imperfect, commonplace, and unsound natures, not to the wise man, who needs not to walk with timid and cautious gait: for he has such confidence in himself that he does not hesitate to go directly in the teeth of Fortune, and never will give way to her.
plain: These words fit ordinary shaky people, not the wise one. He walks without fear, trusts himself, meets hard luck head on, and never gives in.

author: Seneca
text: I will set sail unless anything happens to prevent me, I shall be praetor, if nothing hinders me, my financial operations will succeed, unless anything goes wrong with them.
plain: I will sail unless something stops me, and take office if nothing blocks me. My money plans succeed unless they go wrong.

author: Seneca
text: Yet we gain nothing by getting rid of all personal causes of sadness, for sometimes we are possessed by hatred of the human race.
plain: Clearing every personal cause of sadness still gets you nowhere, because sometimes you hate people as a whole.

author: Seneca
text: I have now, my beloved Serenus, given you an account of what things can preserve peace of mind, what things can restore it to us, what can arrest the vices which secretly undermine it: yet be assured, that none of these is strong enough to enable us to retain so fleeting a blessing, unless we watch over our vacillating mind with intense and unremitting care.
plain: Serenus, I told you what keeps calm, restores it, and stops hidden bad habits. None lasts unless you watch your shaky mind closely.

author: Seneca
text: but what does he gain by so doing if he does not escape from himself? he follows himself and weighs himself down by his own most burdensome companionship.
plain: What does he gain if he never gets away from himself? He tags along with himself and sinks under his own heavy company.

author: Seneca
text: You ask me what I think we had better make use of to help us to support this ennui.
plain: You want to know what I think can help us carry this bored, restless feeling.

author: Seneca
text: To me, my dearest Serenus, Athenodorus seems to have yielded too completely to the times, to have fled too soon: I will not deny that sometimes one must retire, but one ought to retire slowly, at a foot’s pace, without losing one’s ensigns or one’s honour as a soldier: those who make terms with arms in their hands are more respected by their enemies and more safe in their hands.
plain: Serenus, Athenodorus gave way too soon. Retreat slowly without dropping your flag, since people who bargain while armed stay safer and more respected.

author: Seneca
text: Could you anywhere find a miserable city than that of Athens when it was being torn to pieces by the thirty tyrants? they slew thirteen hundred citizens, all the best men, and did not leave off because they had done so, but their cruelty became stimulated by exercise.
plain: Could you find a sadder city than Athens under thirty tyrants? They killed thirteen hundred of the best, and cruelty grew with practice.

author: Seneca
text: We ought, however, first to examine our own selves, next the business which we propose to transact, next those for whose sake or in whose company we transact it.
plain: First look at yourself, then at the job you plan. Then look at the people you do it for or with.

author: Seneca
text: In all cases one should be careful in one’s choice of men, and see whether they be worthy of our bestowing a part of our life upon them, or whether we shall waste our own time and theirs also: for some even consider us to be in their debt because of our services to them.
plain: Choose people with care. See if they deserve some of your life, or if time gets wasted, since some call help a debt.

author: Seneca
text: Let us now pass on to the consideration of property, that most fertile source of human sorrows: for if you compare all the other ills from which we suffer⁠—deaths, sicknesses, fears, regrets, endurance of pains and labours⁠—with those miseries which our money inflicts upon us, the latter will far outweigh all the others.
plain: Now look at property, a rich source of sorrow. Set death, sickness, fear, regret, and pain beside the hurt money brings, and money weighs more.

author: Seneca
text: We shall be pleased with this measure of wealth if we have previously taken pleasure in thrift, without which no riches are sufficient, and with which none are insufficient, especially as the remedy is always at hand, and poverty itself by calling in the aid of thrift can convert itself into riches.
plain: You like this wealth if you first enjoy thrift. Without it no riches are enough, and with it even poverty becomes riches.

author: Seneca
text: You have asked me, Lucilius, why, if the world be ruled by providence, so many evils befall good men?
plain: Lucilius, you asked me why so many bad things hit good people if providence rules the world.

author: Seneca
text: Why do many things turn out badly for good men? Why, no evil can befall a good man; contraries cannot combine.
plain: Why do many things go badly for good people? No real harm can hit a good person, because opposites cannot mix.

author: Seneca
text: Of all these propositions that which I have stated first appears the most difficult to prove, I mean, that the things which we dread and shudder at are to the advantage of those to whom they happen.
plain: Of these claims, the first is hardest to prove. What you dread and shrink from actually helps the people it happens to.

author: Seneca
text: You are a great man; but how am I to know it, if fortune gives you no opportunity of showing your virtue?
plain: You are a great person. I cannot know it if luck never gives you a chance to show it.

author: Seneca
text: Add to this that it is to the advantage of everyone that the best men should, so to speak, be on active service and perform labours: God has the same purpose as the wise man, that is, to prove that the things which the herd covets and dreads are neither good nor bad in themselves.
plain: When the best people work, everyone gains. God and the wise show that what crowds want and fear is neither good nor bad.

author: Seneca
text: He protects and saves them. Does anyone besides this demand that God should look after the baggage of good men also?
plain: He guards them and keeps them safe. Anyone who also asks God to watch good people's bags asks too much.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 1
text: I might truly say, Serenus, that there is as wide a difference between the Stoics and the other sects of philosophers as there is between men and women, since each class contributes an equal share to human society, but the one is born to command, the other to obey.
plain: Serenus, our school and other schools differ like men and women. Each contributes equally, but one is born to lead and one to follow.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 10
text: Since we have now discussed the first part of our subject, let us pass on to the second, in which we will prove by arguments, some of which are our own, but which for the most part are Stoic commonplaces, that the wise man cannot be insulted.
plain: The first part is done, so on to the second. Our points and many shared sayings show a wise person cannot be insulted.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 11
text: Besides this, as most insults proceed from those who are haughty and arrogant and bear their prosperity ill, he has something wherewith to repel this haughty passion, namely, that noblest of all the virtues, magnanimity, which passes over everything of that kind as like unreal apparitions in dreams and visions of the night, which have nothing in them substantial or true.
plain: Most insults come from proud people who handle success badly. A big heart lets him pass them like empty dreams with nothing real in them.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 12
text: In the same spirit in which we deal with boys, the wise man deals with all those whose childhood still endures after their youth is past and their hair is grey.
plain: The wise person treats grey-haired grownups who still act like children the way you treat boys.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 13
text: What, then, is there to prevent your believing this strength of mind to belong to the wise man, when you can see the same thing existing in others, though not from the same cause?⁠—for what physician is angry with a crazy patient? who takes to heart the curses of a fever-stricken one who is denied cold water?
plain: You can believe the wise have this strong mind, as doctors do. No doctor rages at a mad patient or at curses over denied water.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 14
text: Such madness possesses some men that they imagine it possible for an affront to be put upon them by a woman.
plain: Some men are so mixed up they think a woman could insult them.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 15
text: It is from your own weakness that you form your idea of his colossal mind, and when you have thought how much you yourselves could endure to suffer, you place the limit of the wise man’s endurance a little way beyond that.
plain: You picture his huge mind from your own weakness. You guess how much you could bear, then set his limit only a little past yours.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 16
text: Now if even Epicurus, who made more concessions to the body than anyone, takes a spirited tone with regard to injuries, what can appear beyond belief or beyond the scope of human nature amongst us Stoics?
plain: Even Epicurus, softer on the body than anyone, speaks boldly about hurts. Nothing in our view of human nature is hard to believe.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 17
text: Chrysippus says that a man was enraged because someone called him a sea-sheep; we have seen Fidus Cornelius, the son-in-law of Ovidius Naso, weeping in the Senate-house because Corbulo called him a plucked ostrich; his command of his countenance did not fail him at other abusive charges, which damaged his character and way of life; at this ridiculous saying he burst into tears.
plain: Chrysippus tells of rage at being called a sea sheep. Fidus Cornelius wept when called a plucked ostrich, though harsher insults never shook him.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 19
text: We ought not to engage in quarrels and wrangling; we ought to betake ourselves far away and to disregard everything of this kind which thoughtless people do (indeed thoughtless people alone do it), and to set equal value upon the honours and the reproaches of the mob; we ought not to be hurt by the one or to be pleased by the other.
plain: Skip quarrels and step far off from what only thoughtless people do. Crowd praise and blame should neither hurt you nor please you.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 3
text: It has not been my object to decorate the wise man with mere imaginary verbal honours, but to raise him to a position where no injury will be permitted to reach him.
plain: I am not trying to dress the wise person in empty words of praise. I want to lift him where no harm can reach him.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 4
text: Even when powerful men, raised to positions of high authority, and strong in the obedience of their dependents, strive to injure him, all their darts fall as far short of his wisdom as those which are shot upwards by bowstrings or catapults, which, although they rise so high as to pass out of sight, yet fall back again without reaching the heavens.
plain: Powerful people with obedient followers still miss him. Their shots fall short of his wisdom, like arrows that climb out of sight and drop.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 5
text: If you think fit, my Serenus, let us distinguish between injury and insult. The former is naturally the more grievous, the latter less important, and grievous only to the thin-skinned, since it angers men but does not wound them.
plain: Serenus, let us split harm from insult. Harm is heavier, while insult matters less and only stings the thin-skinned, angering them without a wound.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 6
text: Consider now, whether any thief, or false accuser, or headstrong neighbour, or rich man enjoying the power conferred by a childless old age, could do any injury to this man, from whom neither war nor an enemy whose profession was the noble art of battering city walls could take away anything.
plain: Could a thief, false accuser, pushy neighbour, or rich childless man harm him? War and a wall breaker could take nothing from him.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 7
text: A man may become mischievous, and yet do no actual mischief: if a man lies with his own wife as if she were a stranger, he will commit adultery, but his wife will not; if a man gives me poison and the poison lose its strength when mixed with food, that man, by administering the poison, has made himself a criminal, even though he has done no hurt.
plain: You can mean harm yet do none. Treating his wife as a stranger makes him guilty, not her, and poison that fails still marks him.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 8
text: Moreover, justice can suffer nothing unjust, because contraries cannot coexist; but an injury can only be done unjustly, therefore an injury cannot be done to the wise man.
plain: Justice cannot suffer anything unjust, because opposites cannot sit together. Since harm is always unfair, it cannot touch the wise person.

author: Seneca
source: On the Firmness of the Wise Person, chapter 9
text: He therefore endures everything in the same spirit with which he endures the cold of winter and the severities of climate, fevers, diseases, and other chance accidents, nor does he entertain so high an opinion of any man as to suppose that he acts of set purpose, which belongs to the wise man alone.
plain: He bears everything as he bears winter, storms, fever, and accidents. He does not think those men act on purpose, since only the wise do.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 10
text: If I chose to divide this proposition into separate steps, supported by evidence, many things occur to me by which I could prove that the lives of busy men are the shortest of all.
plain: If I split this claim into steps with proof, many reasons show that busy lives are the shortest.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 12
text: Some men’s leisure is busy: in their country house or on their couch, in complete solitude, even though they have retired from all men’s society, they still continue to worry themselves: we ought not to say that such men’s life is one of leisure, but their very business is sloth.
plain: Some rest stays busy. Alone and away, in a country house or on a couch, they still worry, so laziness is the real job.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 14
text: The only persons who are really at leisure are those who devote themselves to philosophy: and they alone really live: for they do not merely enjoy their own lifetime, but they annex every century to their own: all the years which have passed before them belong to them.
plain: Only deep students are truly at rest, and only they truly live. Every century before them is theirs, not just their years.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 15
