text: None of these men will force you to die, but all of them will teach you how to die: none of these will waste your time, but will add his own to it.
plain: None of them will make you die, but each will show you how, and none wastes your time. Each adds his own time to yours.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 16
text: Those men lead the shortest and unhappiest lives who forget the past, neglect the present, and dread the future: when they reach the end of it the poor wretches learn too late that they were busied all the while that they were doing nothing.
plain: People who forget the past, skip now, and fear later live the shortest, saddest lives. Too late they see they stayed busy while doing nothing.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 18
text: Wherefore, my dearest Paulinus, tear yourself away from the common herd, and since you have seen more rough weather than one would think from your age, betake yourself at length to a more peaceful haven: reflect what waves you have sailed through, what storms you have endured in private life, and brought upon yourself in public.
plain: Paulinus, leave the crowd for calmer water. You have sailed more waves than your years show, endured in private and stirred up in public.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 2
text: Why do we complain of Nature? she has dealt kindly with us. Life is long enough, if you know how to use it.
plain: Why complain about nature when she has been kind? Life gives you enough time if you learn how to use it.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 20
text: When, therefore, you see a man often wear the purple robes of office, and hear his name often repeated in the forum, do not envy him: he gains these things by losing so much of his life.
plain: Do not envy the man often in purple, his name ringing in the square. He gains that by giving up much of his life.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 4
text: You will find that the most powerful and highly-placed men let fall phrases in which they long for leisure, praise it, and prefer it to all the blessings which they enjoy.
plain: You will catch top people longing out loud for free time. They praise that rest and choose it over every good thing they hold.

author: Seneca
source: On the Shortness of Life, chapter 9
text: Can anything be mentioned which is more insane than the ideas of leisure of those people who boast of their worldly wisdom?
plain: Nothing sounds more foolish than how people who brag of worldly smarts picture their free time.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: He was once asked how he felt when people abused him, and he said, “As an ambassador feels when he is sent away without an answer.”
plain: When asked how abuse felt, he said he felt like a messenger sent off with no reply.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: On one occasion, when he saw a slave belonging to one of his friends severely bruised, he said to his friend, “I see the footsteps of your anger.”
plain: Once he saw a friend's servant badly bruised, and he told that friend he saw the footprints of his anger.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: A young man was talking a great deal of nonsense, and he said to him, “This is the reason why we have two ears and only one mouth, that we may hear more and speak less.”
plain: A young man talked lots of nonsense. He said two ears and one mouth mean listen more and talk less.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: When he was asked what a friend was, he replied, “Another I.”
plain: Someone asked him to define a friend, and his whole reply was another me.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: Apollonius of Tyre tells us, that when Crates dragged him by the cloak away from Stilpo, he said, “O Crates, the proper way to take hold of philosophers is by the ears; so now do you convince me and drag me by them; but if you use force towards me, my body may be with you, but my mind with Stilpo.”
plain: Crates yanked his cloak to haul him from Stilpo. Take thinkers by the ears, he said, or force takes the body while the mind stays.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 19
text: One of his sayings used to be, that vanity was the most unbecoming of all things, and especially so in the young.
plain: One of his sayings was that vanity is the least fitting thing, especially in the young.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 5
text: Others say, that while he was staying at Athens he heard of a shipwreck, and said, “Fortune does well in having driven us on philosophy.”
plain: Others say that in Athens, after news of a wreck, he spoke. Bad luck did well, he said, to push him toward deep study.

author: Zeno of Citium
source: Diogenes Laertius, Lives of the Philosophers, Book 7, Life of Zeno, section 5
text: So that it is related that he said, “I now find that I made a prosperous voyage when I was wrecked.”
plain: People relate that he said he now sees the wreck as the trip that went well.

author: Plato
text: There you are mistaken: a man who is good for anything ought not to calculate the chance of living or dying; he ought only to consider whether in doing anything he is doing right or wrong—acting the part of a good man or of a bad.
plain: There you are wrong. Someone worth anything skips the odds of living or dying, and only asks if the act is right or wrong.

author: Plato
text: You, my friend,—a citizen of the great and mighty and wise city of Athens,—are you not ashamed of heaping up the greatest amount of money and honour and reputation, and caring so little about wisdom and truth and the greatest improvement of the soul, which you never regard or heed at all?
plain: Friend in mighty Athens, shame on you for piling up money, honour, and fame. You barely heed wisdom, truth, or growth of your mind.

author: Plato
text: For if you kill me you will not easily find a successor to me, who, if I may use such a ludicrous figure of speech, am a sort of gadfly, given to the state by God; and the state is a great and noble steed who is tardy in his motions owing to his very size, and requires to be stirred into life. I am that gadfly which God has attached to the state, and all day long and in all places am always fastening upon you, arousing and persuading and reproaching you.
plain: Kill me and replacing me is hard. I am God's horsefly on a huge slow state, on you all day to wake, persuade, and scold.

author: Plato
text: he must look to himself, and seek virtue and wisdom before he looks to his private interests, and look to the state before he looks to the interests of the state; and that this should be the order which he observes in all his actions.
plain: He must look at himself and seek what is good and wise before private gain. Care for the city before the city's interests.

author: Plato
text: and if I say again that daily to discourse about virtue, and of those other things about which you hear me examining myself and others, is the greatest good of man, and that the unexamined life is not worth living, you are still less likely to believe me.
plain: Checking myself and others each day on how we live is a person's greatest good. A life you never look at is not worth living.

author: Plato
text: I will withdraw them, rather than admit that a man can be temperate or wise who does not know himself; and I am not ashamed to confess that I was in error. For self-knowledge would certainly be maintained by me to be the very essence of knowledge, and in this I agree with him who dedicated the inscription, 'Know thyself!' at Delphi.
plain: I take it back rather than call him wise if he does not know himself. Knowing yourself is the core of knowledge, and Delphi agrees.

author: Plato
text: In questions of just and unjust, fair and foul, good and evil, which are the subjects of our present consultation, ought we to follow the opinion of the many and to fear them; or the opinion of the one man who has understanding?
plain: For right and wrong, decent and ugly, good and bad, which view wins. Do we fear the crowd, or trust one person who understands.

author: Plato
text: And I should like to know whether I may say the same of another proposition--that not life, but a good life, is to be chiefly valued?
plain: I want to know if this other claim matches. A good life, not mere living, is what we value most.

author: Plato
text: Tell me, then, whether you agree with and assent to my first principle, that neither injury nor retaliation nor warding off evil by evil is ever right.
plain: Tell me if you agree with my first rule. Hurting, hitting back, or meeting harm with harm is never right.

author: Plato
text: Then these are the points at issue between us—are they not? I was saying that to do is worse than to suffer injustice?
plain: So this is where we disagree, yes. I said doing wrong is worse than having wrong done to you.

author: Plato
text: NICIAS: I mean to say, Laches, that courage is the knowledge of that which inspires fear or confidence in war, or in anything.
plain: Nicias tells Laches that courage means you know what makes people afraid or sure, in battle or anywhere.

author: Plato
text: The inference at which we arrive for the third or fourth time is, that education is the constraining and directing of youth towards that right reason, which the law affirms, and which the experience of the eldest and best has agreed to be truly right.
plain: Again we land on the same point. Education steers the young toward the right thinking that law and elders call true.

author: Plato
text: And let the figure be composite--a pair of winged horses and a charioteer. Now the winged horses and the charioteers of the gods are all of them noble and of noble descent, but those of other races are mixed; the human charioteer drives his in a pair; and one of them is noble and of noble breed, and the other is ignoble and of ignoble breed; and the driving of them of necessity gives a great deal of trouble to him.
plain: See winged horses and a driver. Godly teams are fully noble, but humans mix one fine horse with one poor, so driving is hard.

author: Plato
text: The divine is beauty, wisdom, goodness, and the like; and by these the wing of the soul is nourished, and grows apace; but when fed upon evil and foulness and the opposite of good, wastes and falls away.
plain: Beauty, wisdom, and goodness are the divine. Those feed the mind's wing so it grows, but evil and ugliness make it shrink and drop.

author: Plato
text: The chariots of the gods in even poise, obeying the rein, glide rapidly; but the others labour, for the vicious steed goes heavily, weighing down the charioteer to the earth when his steed has not been thoroughly trained:--and this is the hour of agony and extremest conflict for the soul.
plain: Divine chariots obey the rein and glide. Others struggle when a wild untrained horse drags the driver down in the mind's worst hour.

author: Plato
text: The right-hand horse is upright and cleanly made; he has a lofty neck and an aquiline nose; his colour is white, and his eyes dark; he is a lover of honour and modesty and temperance, and the follower of true glory; he needs no touch of the whip, but is guided by word and admonition only.
plain: The right horse is white, dark-eyed, and high-necked, nose hooked. He loves honour, modesty, and glory, and words alone guide him, not a whip.

author: Plato
text: And when this has happened several times and the villain has ceased from his wanton way, he is tamed and humbled, and follows the will of the charioteer, and when he sees the beautiful one he is ready to die of fear.
plain: After this happens several times, the wild horse grows humble and tame under the driver. Seeing the beauty, he nearly dies of fear.

author: Plato
text: Then, I said, no man voluntarily pursues evil, or that which he thinks to be evil. To prefer evil to good is not in human nature; and when a man is compelled to choose one of two evils, no one will choose the greater when he may have the less.
plain: Nobody willingly chases what he thinks is bad. Bad over good is not natural, and nobody picks the greater bad when the lesser is there.

author: Plato
text: You know also that the beginning is the most important part of any work, especially in the case of a young and tender thing; for that is the time at which the character is being formed and the desired impression is more readily taken.
plain: You know the start matters most in any work, especially with the young. Character forms then, and the mark you want takes more easily.

author: Plato
text: And would you not say that he is temperate who has these same elements in friendly harmony, in whom the one ruling principle of reason, and the two subject ones of spirit and desire are equally agreed that reason ought to rule, and do not rebel?
plain: You would call him balanced when the parts sit in friendly harmony. Reason leads, spirit and desire agree, and they do not fight its rule.

author: Plato
text: And now, I said, let me show in a figure how far our nature is enlightened or unenlightened:—Behold! human beings living in a underground den, which has a mouth open towards the light and reaching all along the den; here they have been from their childhood, and have their legs and necks chained so that they cannot move, and can only see before them, being prevented by the chains from turning round their heads.
plain: Picture our nature lit or unlit. From childhood, people sit in an underground cave open to light, legs and necks chained, seeing only forward.

author: Plato
text: In the next place, he will regulate his bodily habit and training, and so far will he be from yielding to brutal and irrational pleasures, that he will regard even health as quite a secondary matter; his first object will be not that he may be fair or strong or well, unless he is likely thereby to gain temperance, but he will always desire so to attemper the body as to preserve the harmony of the soul?
plain: Next he trains the body, shuns brutal pleasures, and treats health as second. Looks or strength matter only if they keep his mind in harmony.

author: Plato
text: And in the acquisition of wealth there is a principle of order and harmony which he will also observe; he will not allow himself to be dazzled by the foolish applause of the world, and heap up riches to his own infinite harm?
plain: When gathering wealth he keeps order and harmony too. Foolish applause will not dazzle him into piling riches up to his own endless harm.

author: Plato
text: 'He is a great spirit (daimon), and like all spirits he is intermediate between the divine and the mortal.' 'And what,' I said, 'is his power?' 'He interprets,' she replied, 'between gods and men, conveying and taking across to the gods the prayers and sacrifices of men, and to men the commands and replies of the gods; he is the mediator who spans the chasm which divides them
plain: A great spirit stands between god and human, as spirits do. He ferries prayers up and orders back, and he bridges that gap.

author: Plato
text: SOCRATES: I see, my dear Theaetetus, that Theodorus had a true insight into your nature when he said that you were a philosopher, for wonder is the feeling of a philosopher, and philosophy begins in wonder.
plain: Theaetetus, Theodorus saw your nature truly in calling you a thinker. Wonder is a thinker's feeling, and thinking starts in wonder.
